sections.summary: Drop the beliefs and habits that waste the most study time: learning styles, brain myths, rereading, highlighting, multitasking and speed-reading promises. Test them on your own PSC study and keep a stop-doing list.
sections.content:
## Overview

Dropping a bad habit frees time for good ones. Many PSC aspirants study for long hours and get little back, not because they lack ability, but because their methods feel productive while teaching little. This short module shows what the research says about the most popular beliefs and habits, and asks you to test them yourself.

The result is a stop-doing list and one study session done entirely with active methods, the bridge to Module 3.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain why the learning-styles idea is not supported and choose methods by content
- Name common neuromyths and check any learning claim with three questions
- Explain why rereading and highlighting feel useful but teach little
- Explain the costs of multitasking and the limits of speed reading
- Keep a stop-doing list with a better habit for each item

## Time

About 3 hours in total: 2 hours 15 minutes of lessons and 45 minutes for the module project. Part-time: weeks 1–2, with the module project due in week 2.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M02-L01: Learning styles and other brain myths (about 1 hour)
2. LRN-M02-L02: Rereading, highlighting, multitasking and speed-reading promises (about 1 hour 15 minutes)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **three-question claim check** for any learning claim you meet
- The **match the method to the content** table
- The **study time audit** to see where your minutes go
- Your **stop-doing list**

## Module project: My stop-doing list and one myth-free study session

1. Finalise your stop-doing list from LRN-M02-L02, with a do-instead for each habit.
2. Plan one 50-minute study session on your next PSC topic using only active methods: read once, recall, margin questions, phone out of the room.
3. Run it, and at the end write how many of your margin questions you could answer from memory.
4. Show the list and your result to a study partner or family member and explain one habit you dropped.

**Proof to record:** Your stop-doing list and the notes from your myth-free session with its recall score.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Myths | Still believe a style or myth without checking | Know the myths but not the evidence | Can explain the evidence and checked one claim |
| Habits | No change | One habit changed | Stop-doing list in use, with do-instead habits |
| Session | Not run | Run with some passive time | Run with only active methods and a recall score |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Read the APS speed-reading summary and the parts of Dunlosky's review on rereading and highlighting.
- Write your stop-doing list with four items and keep it where you study.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| The learning-styles claim and the verdict | Matching teaching to your style improves learning: no adequate evidence (Pashler and others, 2008). |
| Two neuromyths besides learning styles | "We use only 10% of our brain" and left-brained versus right-brained learners. |
| Dunlosky's rating of rereading and highlighting | Low utility. |
| A better use of highlighting time | Margin questions answered later from memory. |
| Effect of heavy media multitasking (Ophir and others) | Worse at ignoring distractions, organising memory and switching tasks. |
| The speed-reading verdict | A trade-off between speed and understanding; get faster by becoming a better reader. |
| Three questions for a learning claim | What is the evidence? Who says so and are they selling? Does it agree with reviews? |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Feeling guilty about past habits.** Most students study this way. Notice, replace, move on.
- **Dropping a habit without a replacement.** Every stop needs a do-instead, or the old habit returns.

sections.title: LRN-M02-L01: Learning styles and other brain myths
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Recognise the learning-styles myth and other brain myths, check any learning claim with three questions, and choose methods by the content instead of by "your style". **Time:** about 1 hour (20 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 30 minutes action).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### The learning-styles idea

You have probably heard it from a teacher, a coaching centre or a YouTube channel: everyone has a **learning style**, usually visual, auditory or kinesthetic (learning by doing), and you learn best when lessons match your style. Many people have taken a quiz that told them their type.

The idea sounds respectful and personal. The problem is that it doesn't hold up when it is tested.

### What the research found

In 2008 four psychologists, Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork, reviewed the evidence for the core claim: that matching teaching to a person's style improves learning. They explained what a fair test needs: people with different styles are taught with different methods, then all are tested in the same way. If the theory is right, "visual" learners should learn more from the visual lesson and "auditory" learners from the spoken one.

Very few studies used this design, and those that did mostly contradicted the theory. Their conclusion: there is no adequate evidence base to justify using learning-styles assessments in general education ([Pashler and others, 2008](https://digitalcommons.usf.edu/psy_facpub/1765/)).

Two things are true and often confused with learning styles:

- **People have preferences.** You may enjoy videos more than books. Enjoyment matters for getting started, but it is not the same as learning more.
- **The content decides the best method, for everyone.** Everyone learns Kerala's districts better with a map, the order of events better with a timeline, and English pronunciation better by listening. A map helps a "verbal" learner as much as a "visual" one.

### Other brain myths

In a survey of 242 teachers in the United Kingdom and the Netherlands, Dekker and others (2012) found that 93% and 96% believed that people learn better in their preferred learning style. Around 46% to 48% believed that we use only 10% of our brain, and 86% to 91% believed that differences between left-brained and right-brained learners explain how people learn. The researchers treat all three as **neuromyths**: popular beliefs that brain science doesn't support. Surprisingly, teachers who knew more general facts about the brain believed more myths, probably because they had read more popular material ([Dekker and others, Frontiers in Psychology](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2012.00429/full)).

### Why myths matter for a PSC aspirant

Myths cost time. An "auditory learner" may spend months listening to PSC audio classes and never practise recall. A "right-brained" person may avoid maths. A believer in the 10% myth may buy an app that promises to "unlock the other 90%".

### Three questions for any learning claim

When a video, coaching centre, app or WhatsApp forward makes a claim about learning, ask:

1. **What is the evidence?** A real study compares two methods and tests learning days later, not right after.
2. **Who says so, and are they selling something?** A course, an app or a "secret method"?
3. **Does it match what reviews say?** Check it against Dunlosky's review (Module 3) and the evidence tables in this course.

## Local example

**Joseph sir**, the retired Malayalam teacher who runs a study group at the Thottilpalam panchayat library, noticed that one member, Vinod, spent every evening listening to PSC audio classes on his phone while driving his autorickshaw. "I'm an auditory learner," Vinod said. "Books don't work for me."

Joseph sir suggested a fair test. For one week, Vinod learned half of a Kerala geography topic his usual way, by listening twice. The other half he learned from a map in the SCERT textbook: he looked, then drew the rivers and districts from memory and checked. Both halves got the same 40 minutes.

Two days later the group quizzed him with ten questions on each half. He scored 4 on the listened half and 8 on the map half. Vinod still listens in the autorickshaw, because it keeps him in touch with the subject, but he now follows each audio class with ten minutes of recall from a map or a blank page at home.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Matching teaching to your learning style improves learning | **No good evidence** | Pashler and others (2008): the few properly designed studies mostly contradicted it. |
| Choosing the method by the content (maps for places, timelines for events) | **Moderate** | Supported by research on dual coding and concrete examples (Module 3). It helps everyone, whatever their preference. |
| "We only use 10% of our brain" | **No good evidence** | Listed as a neuromyth by Dekker and others (2012). |
| Left-brained and right-brained learners | **No good evidence** | Listed as a neuromyth by Dekker and others (2012). |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer and Bjork (2008), "Learning Styles: Concepts and Evidence"](https://digitalcommons.usf.edu/psy_facpub/1765/) | Read the abstract: what a fair test of learning styles needs, and what was found | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Dekker et al. (2012), "Neuromyths in Education", Frontiers in Psychology](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2012.00429/full) | Read the abstract and the introduction's description of neuromyths | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [The Learning Scientists: dual coding materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/dual-coding) | Look at the dual coding poster: a method that helps everyone, not one style | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Write down what you have believed about your own learning: a style, a "type", or a subject you think you can't learn.
2. Choose one PSC topic that you usually learn in your preferred way (for example, listening to classes, or only reading).
3. Split it into two halves of similar size. Learn one half your usual way and the other half with a method that suits the content (a map for places, a timeline for history, a worked example for maths, recall practice for facts). Give each half the same time.
4. Two days later, test both halves with 5 to 10 questions each, without looking. Score them.
5. Find one learning claim online or on WhatsApp (an app, a "secret method", a speed-memory course) and check it with the three questions. Write your verdict in three lines.

**Proof to record:** Your two-half test with both scores, and your three-question check of one learning claim.

## Template: match the method to the content

```
| Content in your PSC syllabus | A method that helps everyone |
| --- | --- |
| Places: districts, rivers, national parks, borders | A map: look, draw from memory, check |
| Events and dates: renaissance, freedom struggle | A timeline: draw it from memory, add causes |
| Processes: how a bill becomes law, the water cycle | A flow diagram explained aloud |
| Comparisons: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha, rights and duties | A two-column table filled in from memory |
| Maths and reasoning | Worked examples, then mixed practice |
| Pronunciation and spoken English | Listening and shadowing |
| Lists of facts: articles, awards, firsts | Flashcards with spaced repetition, mnemonics |
```

## Template: three-question claim check

```
CLAIM CHECK        Date: ______
The claim: _________________________________________________
Where I saw it: ____________________________________________
1. Evidence: is there a study that compared methods and tested days later?  yes / no / not shown
   Details: ________________________________________________
2. Who says so, and are they selling something? ______________
3. Does it agree with Dunlosky's review and this course's evidence tables? yes / no
My verdict: believe / doubt / reject.   Why: ________________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Labelling yourself as one type of learner.** Your preferences are real, but they shouldn't limit how you study. Choose methods by the content.
- **Avoiding reading because you are "visual" or "auditory".** PSC exams are written. Reading with recall is a skill you can build (Module 10).
- **Believing a confident coach or a popular video.** Ask the three questions. Confidence and views are not evidence.
- **Testing a method right after studying.** Fair tests are done days later, because short-term performance misleads.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What did Pashler and others (2008) conclude about learning styles?
    - A) There is no adequate evidence base for using learning-styles assessments in education
    - B) Visual learners learn twice as fast from pictures
    - C) Everyone has exactly one learning style
    - D) Learning styles work only for adults
2. You are learning Kerala's rivers. Which method helps best, whatever your preference?
    - A) Only listening to a lecture
    - B) Highlighting the list
    - C) Copying the list ten times
    - D) A map that you draw from memory and check
3. In Dekker and others' survey, who believed more neuromyths?
    - A) Only new teachers
    - B) Teachers with more general knowledge about the brain
    - C) Teachers who knew nothing about the brain
    - D) Nobody believed them
4. Which is the strongest evidence for a learning method?
    - A) A study comparing two methods with a test days later
    - B) A coaching centre's advertisement
    - C) A friend's recommendation
    - D) A video with a million views

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The abstracts of Pashler and others (2008) and Dekker and others (2012)
- **Action:** Test your "learning style" on a split PSC topic and check one learning claim. It is done when your proof is saved: your two-half test with both scores, and your three-question check of one learning claim.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **A.** The few properly designed studies mostly contradicted the matching idea.
2. **D.** The content (places) suits a map, and drawing from memory adds retrieval.
3. **B.** General brain knowledge predicted more myth belief, probably from popular sources.
4. **A.** Fair comparisons with delayed tests show real learning, not short-term performance.

sections.title: LRN-M02-L02: Rereading, highlighting, multitasking and speed-reading promises
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Drop four popular habits that waste study time (rereading, highlighting, multitasking and speed-reading tricks), and replace each with a better use of the same minutes. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 40 minutes action across three sessions).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

In 2013, John Dunlosky and four colleagues reviewed the research on ten common study techniques and rated each one for how useful it is to students ([Dunlosky, American Educator](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky)). Two came out on top: practice testing and spaced practice. Several of the most popular ones came out near the bottom. This lesson covers the habits to drop; Module 3 covers what to do instead.

### 1. Rereading

Rereading is the most common study method, and it was rated **low utility**. The second reading feels smooth and familiar, so you feel you know the material; that feeling is not memory. In Roediger and Karpicke's experiment (LRN-M01-L03), rereaders were the most confident and remembered the least after a week.

**Instead:** read once carefully, close the book, recall, then reread only the parts you missed.

### 2. Highlighting and underlining

Highlighting was also rated **low utility**. It is quick and looks productive, but deciding what to colour is not the same as learning it, and many students highlight half the page.

**Instead:** write a question in the margin for each important point ("Which article abolished untouchability?"). Later, cover the text and answer your own questions. If you like colours, use them after a recall, to mark what you missed.

### 3. Summarising

Writing summaries was rated low utility too, mainly because most students do it badly: they copy sentences instead of putting ideas in their own words. A summary written **from memory**, then checked, is retrieval practice and is worth doing.

### 4. Multitasking

Studying with WhatsApp, YouTube or the TV running is multitasking: your attention switches back and forth. In a Stanford study, people who multitasked heavily with media were worse at ignoring irrelevant information, at keeping items in memory organised, and at switching between tasks ([Ophir, Nass and Wagner, reported by ScienceDaily](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2009/08/090825113133.htm)). Every switch costs time and accuracy, and the study session feels long while little is learned.

**Instead:** single-task blocks of 25 to 50 minutes with the phone out of the room (Module 5).

### 5. Speed-reading promises

Courses and apps promise reading at 1,000 words a minute with full understanding, "photo-reading" or flashing words one by one. A major review led by the reading scientist Keith Rayner found that there is a trade-off between speed and accuracy: when you read much faster, you understand less. Eye movements are not the bottleneck; understanding the language is. Skimming has its uses, but it loses detail. The best way to read faster is to become a better reader, through practice and vocabulary ([APS summary of Rayner and others, 2016](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/news/releases/speed-reading-promises-are-too-good-to-be-true-scientists-find.html)).

**Instead:** read at a comfortable pace for study, skim only when you need the gist or a single fact (Module 10), and build vocabulary (Module 15).

### 6. A myth about notes

You may have heard that handwritten notes always beat typed notes. The famous 2014 study behind that claim was repeated with more students and the advantage did not hold up; what you write matters more than the tool ([The Learning Scientists, 2019](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2019/2/21-1)). Use paper or phone, whichever helps you write questions and recall.

## Local example

**Ashiq** counted his Sunday as a good study day: three hours. He played a PSC class on YouTube at 1.5x speed, kept WhatsApp open on the laptop, and highlighted the class PDF as he went. On Monday a friend asked him five questions from the class. He got one.

He did the time audit from this lesson for three sessions. Over about 4 hours, he spent 52% of the time watching or rereading, 21% highlighting, 18% on the phone, and 9% answering questions. Almost nothing was recall.

For the next two sessions, on topics of the same size, he changed only the method: watch at normal speed once, pause every 10 minutes and write what he remembered, write two margin questions per page, phone in the kitchen. Each session took about the same time. The next day his friend's five-question test gave him 4 and 5 out of 5. He wrote his stop-doing list on a card and kept it inside his notebook cover.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rereading as your main method | **Limited** | Rated low utility by Dunlosky and others (2013): small benefits compared with recall. |
| Highlighting and underlining | **Limited** | Rated low utility: it rarely improves test performance beyond reading alone. |
| Studying while multitasking costs nothing | **No good evidence** | Heavy media multitaskers did worse at filtering distractions, organising memory and switching (Ophir and others, 2009). |
| Speed reading several times faster with full comprehension | **No good evidence** | Rayner and others (2016): a trade-off between speed and understanding; eye movements are not the bottleneck. |
| Handwritten notes always beat typed notes | **Limited** | The 2014 result did not replicate (Learning Scientists, 2019). Content matters more than the tool. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Dunlosky (2013), "Strengthening the Student Toolbox", American Educator](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky) | Read the introduction and the parts on rereading, highlighting and summarisation | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [ScienceDaily (26 August 2009): heavy media multitaskers pay a mental price (Ophir, Nass and Wagner, PNAS)](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2009/08/090825113133.htm) | Read the whole news report on media multitasking | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [APS (14 January 2016): speed-reading promises are too good to be true (Rayner et al.)](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/news/releases/speed-reading-promises-are-too-good-to-be-true-scientists-find.html) | Read the whole news release on speed reading | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [The Learning Scientists blog (21 February 2019): laptop versus longhand notes, a failed replication](https://www.learningscientists.org/blog/2019/2/21-1) | Read the blog post on laptop versus longhand notes | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. For your next three normal study sessions, keep a time audit: every 10 minutes, write what you were mostly doing (reading, rereading, highlighting, watching, recalling, answering questions, explaining, or on the phone).
2. Add up the percentages of passive time (reading again, highlighting, watching, phone) and active time (recalling, answering, explaining).
3. Do two more sessions on topics of similar size, with the same time, but only active methods: read once, recall on a blank page, write margin questions and answer them, phone out of the room.
4. The next day, answer 5 questions on one old-style topic and 5 on one new-style topic, without looking. Compare.
5. Write your stop-doing list (four habits) with a do-instead for each, and keep it where you study.

**Proof to record:** Your three-session time audit with percentages, the two next-day scores, and your stop-doing list.

## Template: study time audit (one line every 10 minutes)

```
Session date: ______  Topic: ______________  Total minutes: ___
Time   | Mostly doing (read / reread / highlight / watch / recall / answer / explain / phone)
0-10   | ______
10-20  | ______
20-30  | ______
30-40  | ______
40-50  | ______
50-60  | ______
Passive minutes ___ (___%)   Active minutes ___ (___%)
```

## Template: stop doing, do instead

```
STOP DOING                         DO INSTEAD
1. Rereading to feel ready         Read once, close the book, recall, reread only the gaps
2. Highlighting whole pages        One margin question per key point, answered later from memory
3. Studying with WhatsApp open     25-50 minute blocks, phone in another room
4. Speed-watching or speed-reading Normal speed, pause every 10 minutes to recall
My own extra: ____________________ ____________________________________________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Counting hours instead of recall.** Three hours of rereading can teach less than one hour of recall. Track what you can recall, not how long you sat.
- **Watching classes at 2x speed and calling it study.** Speed hides how little sticks. Watch at normal speed and stop often to recall.
- **Keeping the phone nearby "just for the dictionary".** Use a paper slip for unknown words and look them up after the block.
- **Paying for speed-reading or memory "secrets".** No method gives several times the speed with full understanding. Spend the money on nothing; the methods in this course are free.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which two techniques did Dunlosky and others rate most useful?
    - A) Summarising and highlighting
    - B) Speed reading and mind maps
    - C) Rereading and highlighting
    - D) Practice testing and spaced practice
2. What is a better use of time than highlighting a page?
    - A) Copying the page
    - B) Reading it aloud three times
    - C) Writing margin questions and answering them later from memory
    - D) Highlighting in two colours
3. What did the Stanford study find about heavy media multitaskers?
    - A) They had better memories
    - B) They were better at everything
    - C) They read faster
    - D) They were worse at ignoring irrelevant information and switching tasks
4. According to Rayner and others, what limits reading speed?
    - A) Understanding the language, not eye movements
    - B) Whether you move your lips
    - C) The size of the font
    - D) Eye movements only
5. What happened when the famous laptop-versus-longhand study was repeated?
    - A) The handwriting advantage did not hold up
    - B) Handwriting won by even more
    - C) Nobody repeated it
    - D) Laptops won clearly

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Dunlosky's review on rereading, highlighting and summarising, and the reports on multitasking and speed reading
- **Action:** Audit three study sessions, test active methods, and write your stop-doing list. It is done when your proof is saved: your three-session time audit with percentages, the two next-day scores, and your stop-doing list.
- **Quiz:** at least 4 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** Practice testing and distributed practice were the only two rated high utility.
2. **C.** Questions turn the page into retrieval practice.
3. **D.** Ophir, Nass and Wagner (2009) found worse filtering, memory organisation and switching.
4. **A.** There is a trade-off between speed and accuracy; better readers are faster because they understand faster.
5. **A.** The replication by Morehead, Dunlosky and Rawson found no reliable advantage; what you write matters more.

sections.title: Module 3: The six evidence-based strategies
sections.summary: Master the six strategies with the best research behind them: retrieval practice, spaced practice, interleaving, elaboration, concrete examples and dual coding. Use each on your PSC subjects, then combine all six in one study session.
sections.content:
## Overview

These six strategies are promoted by The Learning Scientists, a group of cognitive psychologists who turn research into free materials for students and teachers. Two of them, retrieval and spacing, were the only techniques rated high utility in Dunlosky and colleagues' major review; the others are rated moderate or promising. This module is the heart of the course: everything later builds on it.

Each lesson gives you a tool for your learning system, and the last lesson joins them into one session plan you can use every day of your PSC preparation.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Use at least five forms of retrieval practice, and start and end every session with recall
- Run a Revision tab that schedules spaced reviews of your topics
- Build interleaved practice sets and name problem types before solving
- Ask and check how-and-why questions, and make accurate concrete examples
- Draw meaningful visuals from memory and run a 60-minute six-strategy session

## Time

About 8 hours in total: 6 hours 30 minutes of lessons and 1 hour 30 minutes for the module project. Part-time: weeks 2–3, with the module project due in week 3.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M03-L01: Retrieval practice: learn by pulling information out (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
2. LRN-M03-L02: Spaced practice: a revision schedule that beats cramming (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
3. LRN-M03-L03: Interleaving: mix problem types for maths and reasoning (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
4. LRN-M03-L04: Elaboration and concrete examples: ask why, then make it real (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
5. LRN-M03-L05: Dual coding, and one study session that uses all six (about 1 hour 30 minutes)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **revision schedule** (one of the six core tools) and the **Revision** tab with formulas
- The **retrieval sandwich** and **cover-the-options** method
- The **mixed practice set builder**
- The **why-chain sheet** and **concrete example card**
- The **six-strategy session plan** for daily study

## Module project: My six-strategy week

1. Over one week, run at least four six-strategy sessions (60 or 30 minutes) on your PSC subjects.
2. Keep the Revision tab running all week, doing DUE reviews first each day.
3. Keep all session sheets and log each session in the Study Log.
4. At the end of the week, write half a page: which strategy felt hardest, which gave the best two-day scores, and what you will keep doing.

**Proof to record:** Four session sheets, a screenshot of your Revision tab with the week's scores, and your half-page reflection.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Retrieval | Sessions start with reading | Recall used sometimes | Every session starts and ends with recall |
| Spacing | No Revision tab | Tab made but not followed | DUE reviews done first every study day |
| Interleaving | Only chapter-by-chapter practice | Some mixed questions | Mixed sets with types named first |
| Elaboration and examples | Only "what" questions | Why-questions without checking | Checked why-questions and accurate examples |
| Dual coding | No visuals, or copied ones | Visuals sometimes drawn from memory | A meaningful visual drawn from memory in each session |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Do only LRN-M03-L01 and LRN-M03-L02: the retrieval sandwich and the Revision tab.
- Run one 30-minute six-strategy session in the week.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| The six strategies | Retrieval practice, spaced practice, interleaving, elaboration, concrete examples, dual coding. |
| The two techniques rated high utility by Dunlosky and others | Practice testing and distributed (spaced) practice. |
| The retrieval sandwich | Recall at the start of a session (last topic) and at the end (today's topic). |
| Default review gaps for whole topics | 1, 3, 7, 21 and about 60 days, each starting with recall. |
| What interleaving trains | Choosing the right method; name the type before solving. |
| Best elaboration questions | Why? How? How is X different from Y? Then check the answer. |
| Two tips for concrete examples | Use several different examples; check each is accurate. |
| Rule for dual coding | Use meaningful visuals and draw them from memory, then check. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Using one strategy and ignoring the rest.** Retrieval and spacing are the base; add the others where they fit the content.
- **Judging strategies by how easy they feel.** The strongest strategies feel harder. Judge by scores two days or a week later.

sections.title: LRN-M03-L01: Retrieval practice: learn by pulling information out
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Use several forms of retrieval practice on PSC material, and make recall the first and last step of every study session. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 45 minutes action over three sessions).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

Retrieval practice means **learning by pulling information out of your memory**, not by putting it in again. In Module 1 you saw it beat rereading on your own facts. Of the ten techniques Dunlosky and colleagues reviewed, practice testing was one of only two rated **high utility**: it works for many kinds of material, for learners of different ages and abilities, and in real classrooms ([Dunlosky, 2013](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky)).

### Ten ways to retrieve

You don't need a formal test. Anything that makes you produce the answer from memory counts:

1. **Blank-page recall:** close the book and write everything you remember about the topic.
2. **Answer previous-year questions** (PYQs) on the topic.
3. **Cover the options:** read an MCQ's question, cover the four options with your thumb, answer in your head, then uncover and choose.
4. **Flashcards** with spaced repetition (Module 4).
5. **Explain it aloud** without notes, as if teaching (Module 8).
6. **Fill a blank map, timeline or table** from memory: draw Kerala's districts, the order of the Five-Year Plans, the three lists of the Seventh Schedule.
7. **Answer your own margin questions** with the text covered.
8. **The two-minute warm-up:** before a new topic, recall yesterday's.
9. **Quiz a partner,** and let them quiz you (Module 20).
10. **The weekly brain dump:** on Sunday, list everything you studied this week from memory (your weekly review).

### Rules that make retrieval work

- **Retrieve before you reread.** The book opens after you have tried.
- **Always check.** Compare with the source and fix errors straight away, so you don't strengthen a wrong answer.
- **Make it effortful, not impossible.** If you can't recall anything, the material was never learned: study it again first, then retrieve.
- **Keep it low-stakes.** These are practice tests, not judgements of you. Mistakes now are cheap.
- **Recall at the start and end of every session:** the "retrieval sandwich". Start with yesterday's topic; end with today's.

### Why cover the options?

Kerala PSC exams are multiple choice. When you see the options first, you often recognise the answer without being able to recall it, and recognition feels like knowing. Covering the options makes you recall first, then confirms with the options. It turns every MCQ in your guide into harder, more useful retrieval. It is a simple practical tweak; you will check it against your own scores.

## Local example

**Sreeja** had a guide with 1,000 MCQs on the Indian Constitution. She used to read each question with its options, tick the one that looked right and move on. She scored about 70% in practice and 45% in a mock exam with new questions.

She changed one thing: she covered the options with a strip of card. For each question she said her answer aloud, then uncovered. If her answer was among the options and correct, she ticked it; if she had recognised the answer only after seeing the options, she marked it with an R.

On the first day, 40% of her "correct" answers were R's: things she recognised but couldn't recall. Those became her review list and, later, her flashcards. She also began every afternoon slot with a three-minute blank-page recall of the morning's topic. After two weeks, the R's were down to 15%, and her next mock rose to 58%.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retrieval practice (practice testing) | **Strong** | Rated high utility by Dunlosky and others (2013): works across materials, ages and real classrooms. |
| Checking answers after retrieval (feedback) | **Strong** | Feedback corrects errors so they are not strengthened; recommended in the reviews behind this lesson. |
| Covering the options before answering MCQs | **Limited** | A practical tweak that turns recognition into recall. Retrieval in any format helps; judge this one by your own scores. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [The Learning Scientists: retrieval practice materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/retrieval-practice) | Watch the video and download the poster and bookmark | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [RetrievalPractice.org (Pooja Agarwal): free guides and research](https://www.retrievalpractice.org/) | Browse the free guides and read one on retrieval practice strategies | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Dunlosky (2013), "Strengthening the Student Toolbox", American Educator](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky) | Read the section on practice testing | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. For your next three PSC study sessions, use the retrieval sandwich below.
2. Start each session with a 3-minute blank-page recall of the previous session's topic. Check and fix in another colour.
3. Study today's topic in two chunks. After each chunk, close the book and recall for 3 minutes, then check.
4. End with 10 MCQs on today's topic from a previous paper or your guide, using cover-the-options. Mark answers you only recognised with an R.
5. Log each session in your Study Log: Method = retrieval, and what you recalled.

**Proof to record:** Three retrieval sandwich sheets with your recalls, corrections and MCQ scores (with R marks), and the three Study Log rows.

## Template: retrieval sandwich (one study session)

```
RETRIEVAL SANDWICH      Date: ______  Today's topic: ______________

START (3 min): blank-page recall of last session's topic: ______________
   Recalled ___ points; fixed ___ errors; gaps for tomorrow: ___________

MIDDLE: today's topic in two chunks
   Chunk 1: read ___ min -> recall 3 min -> check   [ ]
   Chunk 2: read ___ min -> recall 3 min -> check   [ ]

END: 10 MCQs, options covered first
   Correct ___/10   of which recognised only (R) ___
   Wrong or R questions go to: review list / flashcards / Revision tab
```

## Template: cover-the-options method

```
1. Cover the four options with a strip of card or your thumb.
2. Read the question. Say or write your answer.
3. Uncover. If your answer is there and right: tick.
   If you only knew it once you saw the options: tick and mark R.
   If wrong: mark X and write the right answer with its source.
4. R and X questions are your review list for the next session.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Peeking at the answer after a few seconds.** Give yourself a real try, 20 to 30 seconds for a fact, before checking.
- **Practising only with MCQs and options visible.** Recognition is easier than recall. Cover the options and mix in blank-page recall.
- **Testing only topics you already know well.** Retrieve your weak topics too. That is where the gains are.
- **Never checking answers.** Unchecked errors get stronger. Check every time.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which is a form of retrieval practice?
    - A) Copying the map neatly
    - B) Drawing Kerala's districts on a blank map from memory
    - C) Highlighting district names
    - D) Reading the map again
2. What is the "retrieval sandwich"?
    - A) Reading a topic twice with a break
    - B) A type of flashcard
    - C) Studying between two meals
    - D) Recall at the start of a session (previous topic) and at the end (today's topic)
3. Why cover the options of an MCQ?
    - A) PSC questions have no options
    - B) It saves paper
    - C) It makes the question shorter
    - D) Recognising an answer is easier than recalling it, so covering forces recall
4. You recall nothing at all about a topic. What should you do?
    - A) Study it again first, then retrieve
    - B) Mark it as done
    - C) Skip the topic for good
    - D) Keep trying for an hour

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The Learning Scientists' retrieval practice materials and the practice testing section of Dunlosky's review
- **Action:** Run three retrieval sandwich sessions on your PSC topics. It is done when your proof is saved: three retrieval sandwich sheets with your recalls, corrections and MCQ scores (with R marks), and the three Study Log rows.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** Producing it from memory is retrieval; the others are re-exposure.
2. **D.** Recall begins and ends every session.
3. **D.** It turns recognition into recall and shows you what you only recognise.
4. **A.** Retrieval should be effortful but possible. If nothing comes, the material needs learning first.

sections.title: LRN-M03-L02: Spaced practice: a revision schedule that beats cramming
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Build a Revision tab that schedules spaced reviews of your PSC topics automatically, and follow it for a week. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 40 minutes action plus 10 minutes a day for a week).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### The spacing effect

The same amount of study, spread over several days, is remembered much longer than the same amount crammed into one session. This is the **spacing effect**, and distributed practice is the second technique Dunlosky and colleagues rated **high utility** ([Dunlosky, 2013](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky)).

Cramming does work, for tomorrow. If your test is the next morning, a long session tonight can help. But a PSC exam covers months of material, and the questions come weeks or months after you studied. Cramming loses that race; spacing wins it.

Spacing works together with retrieval. Each time you come back after a gap and recall, you are doing **spaced retrieval practice**: the forgetting curve flattens a little more with every successful recall (Module 1).

### How far apart?

A sensible default for whole topics is **expanding gaps**: review 1 day after first learning, then 3 days, 7 days, 21 days and about 60 days. Each review starts with recall, then a check.

Don't worry about exact numbers. Research shows clearly that spacing beats cramming; it is less clear that one gap pattern is best for everyone. What matters is that you come back, more than once, with gaps that grow.

For single facts (names, dates, article numbers), spacing by hand is too much work. AnkiDroid does it for you in Module 4, adjusting each card's gaps to how well you know it. The revision schedule in this lesson is for **whole topics and skills**: a chapter, a type of maths problem, a grammar rule.

### Making it automatic

Your Learning Workbook gets a **Revision** tab. You type the topic and the date you first studied it; formulas fill in the review dates, show the next one, and mark DUE on the right days. Each day you open the tab, do the DUE reviews first, and log your score.

A daily PSC plan then has two parts: **reviews due today** (do them first, usually 15 to 30 minutes) and **new learning**. If you have to drop something on a bad day, drop new learning, not reviews.

### When you miss a review

Do it as soon as you can and continue the schedule; don't restart. If your score in a review is low (under about 60%), relearn the gaps and restart that topic from the 1-day review.

## Local example

**Anu** studies three PSC subjects in rotation: Kerala history, the Indian Constitution and geography. Before this lesson she "revised" everything in a panic during the last two weeks before an exam.

She made the Revision tab on her phone and entered the twelve topics she had studied in the previous fortnight, using approximate dates. The formulas immediately showed four topics DUE that day, which surprised her: she had forgotten she had studied two of them.

Her new routine starts at 6 a.m. with the DUE topics: for each one, a five-minute blank-page recall, a check against her notes, and a score out of 10 in the "Last score" column. Then she moves to new learning. After a week she had done 19 reviews and her average score had risen from 5.5 to 7. The Kerala renaissance, which she had always found slippery, was at 8 out of 10 on its 7-day review.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Spaced (distributed) practice | **Strong** | Rated high utility by Dunlosky and others (2013), across many kinds of material. |
| Spacing combined with retrieval | **Strong** | Each spaced review that starts with recall strengthens memory more than rereading. |
| Cramming for an exam weeks away | **No good evidence** | It can help a test the next day, but the material fades quickly. |
| One best pattern of gaps (such as 1-3-7-21-60) | **Limited** | Any spacing beats cramming; expanding gaps are a sensible default, not a proven optimum. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [The Learning Scientists: spaced practice materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/spaced-practice) | Watch the video and download the spaced practice poster | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Nicky Case, "How To Remember Anything Forever-ish" (interactive comic, public domain)](https://ncase.me/remember/) | Revisit the part of the comic that explains why gaps should grow | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Dunlosky (2013), "Strengthening the Student Toolbox", American Educator](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky) | Read the section on distributed practice | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Add a Revision tab to your Learning Workbook with the headings and formulas below. Check that the dates appear when you type a first-studied date.
2. Enter every PSC topic you studied in the last two weeks, with approximate first-studied dates, plus today's topic. Aim for at least 8 rows.
3. For the next 7 days, open the tab first thing in your study time and do every DUE review: blank-page recall for 5 minutes, check, score out of 10 (as a %) in "Last score %".
4. Add each new topic you study this week on the day you study it.
5. On day 7, count the reviews you did and work out your average score. Write two lines on what you noticed.

**Proof to record:** A screenshot of your Revision tab with at least 8 topics and 7 days of review scores, and your two lines.

## Template: Revision tab headings

```csv
Topic,First studied,Review 1 (+1 day),Review 2 (+3 days),Review 3 (+7 days),Review 4 (+21 days),Review 5 (+60 days),Next review,Due today?,Last score %
```

## Template: Revision tab formulas

```
In row 2, with the first study date in B2 (type it as a date, e.g. 2026-11-09):
C2: =B2+1
D2: =B2+3
E2: =B2+7
F2: =B2+21
G2: =B2+60
H2: =IF(C2>=TODAY(),C2,IF(D2>=TODAY(),D2,IF(E2>=TODAY(),E2,IF(F2>=TODAY(),F2,IF(G2>=TODAY(),G2,"done")))))
I2: =IF(OR(C2=TODAY(),D2=TODAY(),E2=TODAY(),F2=TODAY(),G2=TODAY()),"DUE","")
Format C2:H2 as dates. Copy row 2 down for every new topic. Sort or filter by column H to see what is coming.
```

## Template: revision schedule (core tool)

```
REVISION SCHEDULE (expanding gaps)
Day 0   Learn it: read, understand, make notes and questions
Day 1   Review 1: blank-page recall, then check and fix
Day 3   Review 2: answer your questions from memory
Day 7   Review 3: mixed practice questions with other topics
Day 21  Review 4: PYQs or a short timed test on this topic
Day 60  Review 5: quick recall; anything you miss goes to AnkiDroid
Every review starts with RECALL, not rereading. Score yourself, and log the
score in the Revision tab. A score under 60% means: re-learn the gaps and
restart the schedule from Day 1 for that topic.
Facts (names, dates, articles, numbers) live in AnkiDroid, which spaces them
for you. This schedule is for whole topics and skills.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Reviewing by rereading.** Every review starts with recall, then a check. Rereading alone wastes the spacing.
- **Skipping a review because "I remember it".** Prove it with a 5-minute recall. If you do, the review is quick.
- **Putting 40 topics in on day one.** Start with your last two weeks. Add new topics daily, and the tab grows at a pace you can manage.
- **Dropping reviews on busy days.** Drop new learning instead. Reviews protect everything you already studied.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Why does cramming fail for a PSC exam that is weeks away?
    - A) Cramming is against the rules
    - B) It only works for maths
    - C) It takes more time than spacing
    - D) Crammed material fades quickly, while spaced study lasts
2. What should every spaced review start with?
    - A) Highlighting the key points
    - B) Rereading the chapter
    - C) Watching a video on the topic
    - D) A recall from memory, then a check
3. On a very busy day, what should you drop first?
    - A) AnkiDroid reviews
    - B) Reviews that are due
    - C) Sleep
    - D) New learning
4. What is the course's default pattern of review gaps for whole topics?
    - A) 30, 60 and 90 days
    - B) Only once, the day before the exam
    - C) 1, 3, 7, 21 and about 60 days
    - D) Every day for a year

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The spaced practice materials and the distributed practice section of Dunlosky's review
- **Action:** Build your Revision tab and follow it for 7 days. It is done when your proof is saved: a screenshot of your Revision tab with at least 8 topics and 7 days of review scores, and your two lines.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** Cramming can help tomorrow's test but not one weeks later.
2. **D.** Spaced retrieval is stronger than spaced rereading.
3. **D.** Reviews protect what you have already learned; new topics can wait a day.
4. **C.** Expanding gaps are a sensible default; any spacing beats cramming.

sections.title: LRN-M03-L03: Interleaving: mix problem types for maths and reasoning
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Build mixed practice sets for PSC maths and reasoning, and learn to name the problem type before you solve it. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 50 minutes action over two days).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Blocked versus interleaved practice

Most maths books teach in **blocks**: a chapter on percentages followed by 30 percentage questions, then a chapter on ratios followed by 30 ratio questions. In blocked practice you always know which method to use before you read the question, because it is the chapter's method.

The exam is different. Question 63 might be a ratio problem, question 64 a time-and-work problem and question 65 a calendar problem. The hardest part is often **choosing the method**, and blocked practice never trains that.

**Interleaving** means mixing different types of problems in one practice session: a percentage question, then a ratio question, then an average question, in no fixed order. You have to identify the type each time.

### What the research says

Dunlosky and colleagues rated interleaved practice **moderate utility**: promising, with the strongest evidence in mathematics and in learning to tell categories apart, and less evidence for other material ([Dunlosky, 2013](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky)). The Learning Scientists include it among their six strategies ([interleaving materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/interleaving)).

Interleaving has a cost you should expect: practice feels harder and slower, and your score during practice may drop. The benefit shows up later, in tests with mixed questions, which is exactly what a PSC paper is.

### How to interleave

1. **Learn each type first.** Use worked examples and a few blocked questions when a type is new (Module 1). Interleave once you know two or more types.
2. **Mix related types that are easy to confuse:** percentage and profit-and-loss, ratio and partnership, speed and time-and-work, simple and compound interest.
3. **Name the type before solving.** Write "ratio: compare parts" or "time and work: add the rates" before you calculate. This is the skill you are training.
4. **Mix old and new.** Include types from earlier weeks; that also gives you spacing.
5. **Interleave subjects in a day:** a block of GK, then a block of maths, then English, instead of a whole day on one subject.

The idea also helps outside maths when topics are easy to confuse: Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties; the rivers of Kerala and those of Karnataka; similar-sounding award names. Mixed questions force you to tell them apart.

## Local example

**Ashiq** is good at maths. He practised by chapter: 30 percentage questions in 25 minutes, 30 ratio questions in 20. In his first full mock, the mental ability section went badly. He knew every method, but he lost time staring at mixed questions, unsure which method each one needed, and he used the percentage method on a profit-and-loss question with a twist.

He built mixed sets of 12 questions from four chapters he had studied: percentages, profit and loss, ratio and proportion, and averages. He wrote each question number on a slip of paper, shuffled the slips, and solved in that order. Before solving, he wrote the type and the method in a few words.

His first mixed set took 22 minutes, and he named the type correctly for 9 of 12. By the fourth set, a week later, he took 15 minutes and named all 12. In his next mock he finished the mental ability section with five minutes to spare.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Interleaved practice for maths and problem types | **Moderate** | Rated moderate utility by Dunlosky and others (2013); strongest evidence in mathematics and category learning. |
| Interleaving easily confused topics in GK | **Limited** | Less research outside maths and categories; useful in practice for telling similar facts apart. |
| Practice scores drop at first | **Moderate** | Interleaving feels harder during practice; its benefit shows in later mixed tests. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| [Dunlosky (2013), "Strengthening the Student Toolbox", American Educator](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky) | Read the section on interleaved practice | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose four maths or reasoning question types you have already studied, from your PSC syllabus (for example percentages, profit and loss, ratio, averages; or series, coding, directions, blood relations).
2. Pick three questions of each type from your guide or previous papers: 12 in all. Write their numbers on slips of paper and shuffle them.
3. Solve in the shuffled order. Before each one, write the type and the method in a few words. Time the whole set.
4. Mark each question twice: type named correctly? answer correct?
5. The next day, build a second mixed set of 12 from the same four types (new questions) and repeat. Compare time, types named and answers correct.

**Proof to record:** Your two mixed sets with type labels, workings, both marks and the times.

## Template: mixed practice set builder

```
MIXED SET #___     Date: ______   Types in this set: A ______ B ______ C ______ D ______
Shuffled order: ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___ ___

Q  | Type I named      | Method in a few words         | Type right? | Answer right?
1  | _________________ | _____________________________ | Y / N       | Y / N
2  | _________________ | _____________________________ | Y / N       | Y / N
...
12 | _________________ | _____________________________ | Y / N       | Y / N
Time: ___ min   Types named right ___/12   Answers right ___/12
Confused pairs (e.g. percentage vs profit-and-loss): _______________________
```

## Template: easily confused pairs to mix (PSC)

```
| Maths and reasoning | GK and language |
| --- | --- |
| Percentage and profit and loss | Fundamental Rights, Directive Principles and Fundamental Duties |
| Ratio and partnership | Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha |
| Speed-distance and time and work | Kerala rivers and their districts |
| Simple and compound interest | Similar award names and their fields |
| Number series and letter series | Synonyms and antonyms |
```

## Common mistakes

- **Interleaving a type you have not learned yet.** Learn each type with worked examples first; mix once you know two or more.
- **Giving up because it feels slow.** Slower practice is the price of better exam performance. Compare scores after a week.
- **Solving before naming the type.** Naming the type is the skill. Write it first, every time.
- **Mixing only unrelated topics.** Mix types that are easy to confuse; that is where interleaving helps most.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What skill does interleaving train that blocked practice does not?
    - A) Reading questions aloud
    - B) Writing faster
    - C) Remembering formulas
    - D) Choosing the right method for each question
2. How did Dunlosky and colleagues rate interleaved practice?
    - A) High utility for everything
    - B) Low utility
    - C) Moderate utility, strongest in maths and category learning
    - D) Not reviewed
3. When should you start interleaving a new maths type?
    - A) After learning it with worked examples and a few practice questions
    - B) Never
    - C) Only on exam day
    - D) Before seeing any example
4. Your practice score drops when you start interleaving. What does that most likely mean?
    - A) The questions are wrong
    - B) It is the expected cost; the benefit shows in later mixed tests
    - C) You should go back to blocked practice for good
    - D) Interleaving does not work for you

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The interleaving materials and the interleaved practice section of Dunlosky's review
- **Action:** Solve two shuffled mixed sets of PSC maths or reasoning questions, naming each type first. It is done when your proof is saved: your two mixed sets with type labels, workings, both marks and the times.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** In blocked practice the chapter tells you the method; in exams you must choose.
2. **C.** It is promising, with most evidence in maths and telling categories apart.
3. **A.** Learn each type first, then mix.
4. **B.** Interleaving feels harder at first; judge it by mixed tests a week later.

sections.title: LRN-M03-L04: Elaboration and concrete examples: ask why, then make it real
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Turn PSC facts into connected knowledge with how-and-why questions, and make abstract ideas memorable with accurate examples from Kerala life. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (15 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 40 minutes action plus a 10-minute check two days later).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Elaboration: ask how and why

**Elaboration** means explaining and connecting ideas: asking how and why something is true, and how it relates to what you already know. Dunlosky and colleagues rated two forms of it, **elaborative interrogation** (asking "why?") and **self-explanation**, as **moderate utility**: promising, with good evidence for factual learning ([Dunlosky, 2013](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky)).

It works because a fact connected to other facts has more ways to be found again (Module 1). Compare:

- "Kerala state was formed on 1 November 1956." One isolated fact.
- "**Why** then? Because the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 redrew states on language lines, and Malayalam-speaking Travancore-Cochin and Malabar were joined." Now the date hangs on a reason, a law and a map.

Good elaboration questions for PSC topics:

- **Why** did this happen? **Why** is this true?
- **How** does it work? **How** did it change things?
- **How is X different from Y?** (Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles: the first can be enforced in court, the second cannot.)
- **What would happen if** it were not so?
- **How does this connect to** something I already know?

Always **check your answers against the source**. Elaboration with a wrong explanation can make a wrong idea stick.

### Concrete examples: make it real

Abstract ideas (federalism, inflation, secularism, a fundamental duty, GDP) are hard to remember as definitions. A **concrete example** is a specific case that shows the idea. The Learning Scientists list concrete examples as one of their six strategies ([concrete examples materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/concrete-examples)). Three tips:

1. **Use more than one example,** and make them different. Then ask what they have in common: that common thread is the idea.
2. **Use examples from your own life in Kerala.** Inflation: the price of a meal at your local hotel this year compared with five years ago. The Concurrent List: education, where both Parliament and the state legislature can make laws.
3. **Check that your example is accurate.** A wrong example teaches a wrong idea. Confirm it in your textbook.

### Using both together

Read a paragraph, ask a why-question, answer it from memory in your own words, give an example, then check. This is slower than reading, and it is supposed to be: you are building connections that will hold the facts for months.

## Local example

**Joseph sir**'s study group uses "why chains" for geography. One evening the topic was the monsoon. Instead of memorising "the south-west monsoon reaches Kerala first", they asked a chain of questions and answered each from memory before checking the SCERT textbook:

- Why does the monsoon reach Kerala first? Because Kerala is at the south-western tip of the peninsula, the first land the moist south-west winds meet.
- Why does it rain so much on our side? Because the Western Ghats force the moist winds to rise and cool.
- So how is the other side of the Ghats different? It gets far less rain; it is in the rain shadow.

Then each member gave a concrete example from their own experience: Vinod described the heavy rain at Kuttiady compared with what his cousin sees across the Ghats in Karnataka. One member's answer about where the winds come from turned out to be wrong when they checked, and they corrected it together. Two days later, all five answered the group's five monsoon questions without notes.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Elaborative interrogation (asking why) | **Moderate** | Rated moderate utility by Dunlosky and others (2013), with good evidence for learning facts. |
| Self-explanation | **Moderate** | Rated moderate utility; explored further in Module 8. |
| Concrete examples, especially several different ones | **Moderate** | One of the Learning Scientists' six strategies; works best with varied examples and the common idea made explicit. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [The Learning Scientists: elaboration materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/elaboration) | Watch the video and download the elaboration poster | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [The Learning Scientists: concrete examples materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/concrete-examples) | Watch the video and download the concrete examples poster | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Dunlosky (2013), "Strengthening the Student Toolbox", American Educator](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky) | Read the sections on elaborative interrogation and self-explanation | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose a PSC topic with causes, processes or comparisons: a period of Kerala history, a geography process or a part of the Constitution.
2. Write 10 how-or-why questions about it. Answer each from memory in one or two sentences, then check the textbook and correct in another colour.
3. Write 3 "how is X different from Y?" questions on things in the topic that are easy to confuse, and answer them the same way.
4. Pick 3 abstract terms from your syllabus (for example federalism, inflation, secularism, a fundamental duty, GDP). Write two different concrete examples for each, from Kerala life where you can, and check each against your textbook.
5. Two days later, answer 5 of your why-questions from memory, without looking. Score them.

**Proof to record:** Your why-question sheet with corrections, the 3 comparisons, the 6 examples and your two-day score.

## Template: why-chain sheet

```
WHY-CHAIN SHEET      Topic: ______________  Source: ______________ page ___
Q1  Why ______________________________?  My answer: _________________ Checked [ ] Fixed: ____
Q2  How ______________________________?  My answer: _________________ Checked [ ] Fixed: ____
...
Q10 _________________________________?  My answer: _________________ Checked [ ] Fixed: ____

COMPARE
How is ______ different from ______? _________________________________________
How is ______ different from ______? _________________________________________
How is ______ different from ______? _________________________________________

Two-day check (no looking): ___/5
```

## Template: concrete example card

```
ABSTRACT IDEA: ______________   Definition in my words: _______________________
Example 1 (from Kerala life): ____________________________________________
Example 2 (different kind): _____________________________________________
What both examples have in common (the idea): _____________________________
Checked in: ______________ page ___
```

## Common mistakes

- **Accepting your own explanation without checking.** A confident wrong answer sticks too. Check every answer against the source.
- **Vague examples ("like in daily life").** Name a specific case: a place, a price, a law, a person.
- **Using only one example.** Two different examples show what the idea really is; one example can mislead.
- **Asking only "what" questions.** "What" checks the fact; "why" and "how" build the connections that hold it.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which question is an elaborative why-question?
    - A) When was Kerala formed?
    - B) Who was the first Chief Minister of Kerala?
    - C) How many districts does Kerala have?
    - D) Why did the 1956 reorganisation create Kerala on language lines?
2. What is the main risk of elaboration?
    - A) It takes no effort
    - B) Building on a wrong explanation if you don't check it
    - C) It works only for maths
    - D) It replaces all other study
3. What makes concrete examples most useful?
    - A) Examples without checking them
    - B) Examples from another country only
    - C) Several different examples, with the common idea made clear
    - D) One vivid example repeated often
4. How did Dunlosky and colleagues rate elaborative interrogation?
    - A) Low utility
    - B) Moderate utility
    - C) Harmful
    - D) High utility

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The elaboration and concrete examples materials and Dunlosky's sections on elaborative interrogation and self-explanation
- **Action:** Write and answer 10 why-questions, 3 comparisons and 6 checked examples on a PSC topic. It is done when your proof is saved: your why-question sheet with corrections, the 3 comparisons, the 6 examples and your two-day score.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** It asks for a reason and connects the date to a law and an idea.
2. **B.** Always check your answers against the source.
3. **C.** Varied examples show what the idea is, not just one case of it.
4. **B.** It is promising, with good evidence for factual learning.

sections.title: LRN-M03-L05: Dual coding, and one study session that uses all six
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Combine words with maps, timelines and diagrams, and run a complete 60-minute study session that uses all six strategies on one PSC topic. **Time:** about 1 hour 30 minutes (20 minutes reading, 25 minutes resources, 60-minute study session plus a 15-minute check two days later).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Dual coding: words plus pictures

**Dual coding** means combining words with visuals: a map, a timeline, a flowchart, a table or a diagram. You then have two connected ways to find the memory, a verbal one and a visual one. The Learning Scientists list it among their six strategies ([dual coding materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/dual-coding)).

Dual coding is **not** about learning styles (Module 2). A map helps everyone learn where places are. A timeline helps everyone learn the order of events.

Choose the visual by the content:

| PSC content | Visual | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Places | Map | Kerala's 14 districts from north to south; national parks |
| Order of events | Timeline | The Kerala renaissance: 1888, 1903, 1924, 1936 |
| Processes | Flowchart | How a bill becomes law; how a PSC rank list is made |
| Comparisons | Table | Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; rights and duties |
| Parts of a whole | Labelled diagram | Parts of the heart; layers of the atmosphere |
| Hierarchies | Tree | The court system; local government tiers |

Three rules make dual coding work:

1. **The picture must carry meaning.** A decorative photo of a temple doesn't help you remember the Temple Entry Proclamation; a timeline that places it after the Vaikom and Guruvayur satyagrahas does.
2. **Draw it from memory, then check.** Drawing a timeline from memory is dual coding and retrieval at once. Copying a diagram neatly is mostly copying.
3. **Keep it simple.** Boxes, arrows, a few words. You are not making art, and an overloaded diagram adds cognitive load (Module 1).

Be careful with one related idea: Dunlosky and colleagues rated **imagining pictures while reading text** as low utility ([Dunlosky, 2013](https://www.aft.org/ae/fall2013/dunlosky)). Real, meaningful visuals that you look at and draw are a different thing.

### One session, six strategies

Each strategy is good alone; together they make a study session that is hard to beat. Here is a 60-minute plan for one PSC topic:

| Minutes | What you do | Strategies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0–5 | Blank-page recall of the last session's topic; check | Retrieval, spacing |
| 5–25 | Learn the new topic in chunks; ask why and how; give your own example for each idea | Elaboration, concrete examples |
| 25–35 | Close the book; draw a map, timeline or diagram of it from memory; check and fix | Dual coding, retrieval |
| 35–50 | Mixed practice: 10 questions from this topic and two older ones, options covered | Interleaving, retrieval |
| 50–55 | Check answers; note errors; add the topic to the Revision tab | Spacing |
| 55–60 | Write three margin questions for tomorrow's warm-up | Retrieval (planned) |

The same structure works in 30 minutes: halve every part.

## Local example

**Anu** chose the Kerala renaissance for her six-strategy session. She began with a five-minute recall of yesterday's topic, the Travancore kings, and fixed two errors.

Then she studied four events with why-questions: why Sree Narayana Guru's consecration of a Shiva idol at Aruvippuram in 1888 was revolutionary; why the SNDP Yogam was founded in 1903; what the Vaikom Satyagraha of 1924 demanded; and what the Temple Entry Proclamation of 1936 changed. For each she wrote one line in her own words and one example of what the change meant for an ordinary person.

She closed the book and drew a timeline from memory with the four dates and the causes between them. She had placed two events in the wrong order; she fixed them in red. Next came ten mixed MCQs from the renaissance, the Travancore kings and the freedom struggle, with options covered. She scored 7, noted the three errors and added the topic to her Revision tab.

Two days later she redrew the timeline from memory, this time with no errors, and scored 9 out of 10 on new questions.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Meaningful visuals combined with words (dual coding) | **Moderate** | One of the Learning Scientists' six strategies; the visual must carry the meaning, not decorate. |
| Imagining pictures while reading text | **Limited** | Rated low utility by Dunlosky and others (2013). Draw real visuals instead. |
| Combining the six strategies in one session | **Limited** | Little research on this exact package; each part has its own evidence, and the strongest parts are retrieval and spacing. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [The Learning Scientists: dual coding materials](https://www.learningscientists.org/dual-coding) | Watch the video and download the dual coding poster | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [The Learning Scientists: free posters, slides and bookmarks for the six strategies](https://www.learningscientists.org/downloadable-materials) | Download the six-strategy bookmarks (or posters) and keep them where you study | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [College Success, chapter 6: Studying, Memory, and Test Taking](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/06%3A_Studying_Memory_and_Test_Taking) | Read 6.2 Studying, and compare its advice with the six strategies | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Choose a new PSC topic for one 60-minute session.
2. Run the six-strategy session plan below, ticking each part as you finish it.
3. Make your visual (map, timeline, flowchart, table or diagram) from memory in the 25–35 minute part, then check and fix it.
4. Add the topic to your Revision tab.
5. Two days later, redraw the visual from memory without looking, and answer 5 new questions on the topic. Score both.

**Proof to record:** Your session plan with all six parts ticked, both versions of your visual drawn from memory, and the two-day scores.

## Template: six-strategy study session (60 minutes)

```
SIX-STRATEGY SESSION     Date: ______  Topic: ______________
[ ] 0-5    Warm-up recall of last topic (__________): recalled ___ points, fixed ___
[ ] 5-25   Learn in chunks: why/how question + my own example for each idea
           1. ______________________  2. ______________________  3. ____________
[ ] 25-35  Visual from memory: map / timeline / flowchart / table / diagram
           Errors found when checking: ___
[ ] 35-50  Mixed practice: 10 questions (this topic + __________ + __________)
           Correct ___/10, recognised only (R) ___
[ ] 50-55  Errors noted; topic added to the Revision tab
[ ] 55-60  Three margin questions for tomorrow:
           1. _____________________ 2. _____________________ 3. _____________________
Two-day check: visual redrawn with ___ errors; new questions ___/5
```

## Template: choose your visual

```
Is it about WHERE?         -> map
Is it about WHEN or ORDER? -> timeline
Is it about HOW (steps)?   -> flowchart
Is it about COMPARING?     -> two- or three-column table
Is it about PARTS?         -> labelled diagram
Is it about LEVELS?        -> tree
Rule: draw it from memory first, then check, then fix in another colour.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Decorating notes with pictures that carry no meaning.** Every visual should show where, when, how, what differs, or what the parts are.
- **Copying a diagram instead of drawing it from memory.** Look, close the book, draw, check. Copying feels productive and teaches little.
- **Cramming too much onto one visual.** One visual, one idea. Make two simple ones rather than one crowded one.
- **Skipping the mixed practice part to save time.** It is where retrieval and interleaving happen. Shorten the other parts instead.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which visual best suits the order of events in the Kerala renaissance?
    - A) A pie chart
    - B) A timeline
    - C) A labelled diagram of a building
    - D) A photo of a temple
2. Is dual coding the same as matching a "visual learning style"?
    - A) Yes, it only helps visual learners
    - B) No, it only helps auditory learners
    - C) No: meaningful visuals help everyone learn content such as places and sequences
    - D) Yes, and it harms auditory learners
3. What did Dunlosky and colleagues rate as low utility?
    - A) Interleaved practice in maths
    - B) Imagining pictures while reading text
    - C) Distributed practice
    - D) Practice testing
4. In the 60-minute six-strategy session, what happens in minutes 35–50?
    - A) Rereading the chapter
    - B) A break
    - C) Drawing decorative pictures
    - D) Mixed practice questions from this topic and older ones

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The dual coding materials, the six-strategy bookmarks and College Success 6.2 Studying
- **Action:** Run one 60-minute six-strategy session with a visual drawn from memory, and check it two days later. It is done when your proof is saved: your session plan with all six parts ticked, both versions of your visual drawn from memory, and the two-day scores.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **B.** A timeline shows order and the gaps between events.
2. **C.** The content decides the visual, not a learning style.
3. **B.** Imagery for text learning was rated low; real, meaningful visuals are different.
4. **D.** Mixed questions combine interleaving and retrieval, with spacing for the older topics.
