sections.title: Module 6: Motivation, procrastination and habits
sections.summary: Understand why you procrastinate, and build habits that run on days when motivation is low: if-then plans, tiny habits anchored to your routines, small rewards, and a restart protocol for bad weeks.
sections.content:
## Overview

PSC preparation is a long race, and most aspirants don't fail because of ability; they fail because study becomes irregular. This module treats procrastination as a feeling to manage, not a character flaw, and gives you the tool with some of the strongest evidence in behaviour research: the if-then plan.

The result is a small habit system, tracked in the free Loop app, with your reasons, rewards and a plan for restarting.

## Outcomes

By the end of this module you can:

- Explain procrastination as short-term mood repair and find your own triggers
- Use the five-minute start and shrink tasks you avoid
- Write if-then plans for habits and obstacles, and anchor tiny habits to routines
- Track habits in Loop and use rewards and streaks wisely
- Restart quickly after a bad week with a written protocol

## Time

About 4 hours 30 minutes in total: 3 hours 30 minutes of lessons and 1 hour for the module project. Part-time: weeks 7–8, with the module project due in week 8.

## Lessons

1. LRN-M06-L01: Why we procrastinate (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
2. LRN-M06-L02: Implementation intentions and tiny habits (about 1 hour 15 minutes)
3. LRN-M06-L03: Rewards, streaks and restarting after a bad week (about 1 hour)

## Tools this module adds to your learning system

- The **procrastination log** and **task shrinker**
- The **if-then planner** and **Loop Habit Tracker** with three habits
- Your **reason card**, **reward menu** and **restart protocol**

## Module project: My habit system

1. Show at least 14 days of Loop records for your three habits.
2. Review your if-then plans: keep those that worked, rewrite those that didn't, and add one for your weakest day.
3. Put your reason card, reward menu and restart protocol together on one page in your notebook.
4. Explain your habit system to your study partner or a family member, and ask them to check in with you once a week for the next month.

**Proof to record:** A Loop screenshot with 14 or more days, your updated if-then plans and your one-page habit system.

## Self-assessment rubric

Score yourself honestly after the project. Move on when no row is a 1 and at least half the rows are 3. If a row is a 1, redo that part first.

| Criterion | 1: Not yet | 2: Getting there | 3: Ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Understanding procrastination | Still "I'm lazy" | Know the triggers in general | Found my own triggers in a log and acted on them |
| If-then plans | None | Vague plans | Specific plans for habits and obstacles, revised after 14 days |
| Tracking | Not tracked | Tracked a few days | 14 or more days in Loop |
| Restarting | No plan | A plan in my head | A written protocol, used at least once if needed |

## Short on time?

The minimum version, for weeks when PSC study, work or family leaves little time:

- Write three if-then plans and add one habit (daily AnkiDroid) to Loop.
- Keep the restart protocol in your notebook.

## Revision flashcards

Cover the right-hand column, read the front, say the answer aloud, then check. Add the ones you miss to AnkiDroid (from Module 4 on).

| Front (say the answer aloud) | Back |
| --- | --- |
| Procrastination in one line (Sirois and Pychyl) | Short-term mood repair: avoiding an unpleasant task to feel better now. |
| The five-minute start | Promise only five minutes; most people keep going. |
| Implementation intention | "If [situation], then I will [action]." |
| Effect of if-then plans (Gollwitzer and Sheeran) | Medium to large (d = 0.65) across 94 tests. |
| Average time to form a daily habit (Lally) | About 66 days, from 18 to 254. |
| Tiny habit with an anchor | "After I pour my morning tea, I will open AnkiDroid and do 10 cards." |
| Streak rule | Never miss twice. |
| First step after a bad week | Forgive yourself, then do the tiny version today. |

## Top mistakes in this module

- **Reading about habits without writing any if-then plans.** The plan is one sentence. Write it now.
- **Building a perfect system and abandoning it after one bad week.** The restart protocol is part of the system.

sections.title: LRN-M06-L01: Why we procrastinate
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Explain procrastination as short-term mood repair, find your own triggers with a procrastination log, and use the five-minute start on a task you have been avoiding. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 30 minutes action plus a 5-day log).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Procrastination is not laziness

**Procrastination** means delaying something you intended to do, even though you expect the delay to cost you. Almost everyone does it, and PSC preparation, with its long syllabus and distant exam dates, invites it.

Researchers Fuschia Sirois and Timothy Pychyl describe procrastination as a problem of **short-term mood repair**. When a task feels unpleasant (boring, confusing, frightening), avoiding it makes you feel better right now. The bill goes to your **future self**, who has less time and more stress ([Sirois and Pychyl, 2013](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/91793/)). That is why "just be disciplined" rarely works: the problem is a feeling, so the fix has to deal with the feeling.

### What makes a PSC task feel bad

Notice which of these describe the tasks you put off:

- **Boring:** long lists of static GK facts
- **Hard or unclear:** a maths topic where you don't know the method
- **Big or vague:** "finish the Constitution", "start current affairs"
- **Frightening:** a full mock test that might show a low score
- **No reward now:** the exam is months away; Reels are right here
- **Unsure where to start:** a new subject with no plan

### Five ways to make starting easier

1. **Shrink the task.** Not "do maths" but "open the guide at page 34 and do five percentage questions". A small, specific task feels less threatening.
2. **The five-minute start.** Promise yourself only five minutes. Once started, most people continue; if you don't, you still did five minutes.
3. **Remove friction the night before.** Book open at the right page, phone charging in another room, pen on the table.
4. **Name the feeling.** "I feel bored" or "I'm afraid of this mock". Naming it makes it smaller, and you can start anyway.
5. **Talk to your future self.** Write one line from "exam-day me" to "today me": what you will be glad you did.

### Forgive yourself

One study followed 134 first-year university students through two sets of exams. Students who forgave themselves for procrastinating before the first exams felt less negative afterwards and procrastinated less before the second exams ([BPS Research Digest on Wohl, Pychyl and Bennett, 2010](https://bps.org.uk/research-digest/cure-procrastination-forgive-yourself)). Harsh self-criticism makes the next task feel even worse, which feeds the cycle. Forgiving yourself is not excusing the delay; it is clearing the way to start again.

## Local example

**Anu** kept postponing the mental ability section of her syllabus. Every evening she planned to start "time and work" and every evening she reorganised her notes, tidied her desk, or did another round of GK instead.

Her five-day procrastination log made the pattern clear. Every delay was on maths, the feeling was always the same ("I'll get them wrong and feel stupid"), and her escape was always a task that felt productive. The trigger was fear, not laziness.

She shrank the task to "two worked examples of time and work from the guide, then one problem of my own", and used the five-minute start. On the first evening she stopped after the five minutes. On the second she did 20 minutes. By the fourth she finished the chapter's first exercise. She also wrote a short note forgiving herself for the three weeks of delay, and kept it in the back of her maths notebook. "It was the feeling of failing I was avoiding," she wrote, "not the maths."

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Procrastination as short-term mood repair | **Moderate** | A well-supported view in procrastination research, set out by Sirois and Pychyl (2013). |
| Self-forgiveness reduces later procrastination | **Limited** | One study of 134 students (Wohl, Pychyl and Bennett, 2010); encouraging but not yet strong. |
| Shrinking tasks and the five-minute start | **Limited** | Practical methods consistent with research on task aversion and if-then plans (LRN-M06-L02). |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Sirois and Pychyl (2013), "Procrastination and the Priority of Short-Term Mood Regulation" (free author copy)](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/id/eprint/91793/) | Read the abstract and introduction: why procrastination is about mood | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [BPS Research Digest (4 May 2010): to cure procrastination, forgive yourself (Wohl, Pychyl and Bennett)](https://bps.org.uk/research-digest/cure-procrastination-forgive-yourself) | Read the summary of the self-forgiveness study | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [College Success, chapter 3: Managing Your Time and Priorities (procrastination, time management, goals)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/03%3A_Managing_Your_Time_and_Priorities) | Read 3.3 Procrastination: The Enemy Within | 20 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| ["Learning How to Learn" by Barbara Oakley and Terrence Sejnowski (Coursera, free to enrol; certificate paid)](https://www.coursera.org/learn/learning-how-to-learn) | Optional, later: Module 3 (Procrastination and Memory) of Learning How to Learn | About 3 hours | verified 2026-11-03; check current rules |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. For five days, keep a procrastination log: each time you delay a planned study block, note the task, the feeling, the trigger type, what you did instead, and for how long.
2. Pick the study task you avoided most. Shrink it to a first step of five minutes or less, written down exactly (book, page, number of questions).
3. Do the five-minute start three times on that task. After each, note whether you stopped at five minutes or kept going, and for how long.
4. The night before each start, remove friction: book open, pen out, phone charging in another room.
5. Write a short self-forgiveness note for one past delay, ending with what you will do next time.

**Proof to record:** Your 5-day procrastination log, notes from your three five-minute starts, and your self-forgiveness note.

## Template: procrastination log

```
PROCRASTINATION LOG
Day | Task I delayed        | Feeling (bored / confused / afraid / tired / other) | Trigger type | What I did instead | How long
1   | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________ | __________________ | ____
2   | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________ | __________________ | ____
3   | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________ | __________________ | ____
4   | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________ | __________________ | ____
5   | ____________________ | ____________________ | ____________ | __________________ | ____
Trigger types: boring, hard or unclear, big or vague, frightening, no reward now, unsure where to start
Pattern I see: ____________________________________________________________
```

## Template: task shrinker

```
BIG TASK: ______________________________________ (e.g. "start time and work")
First step of 5 minutes or less (book, page, exact action):
______________________________________________________________________
Friction removed the night before: [ ] book open  [ ] pen out  [ ] phone away
Five-minute starts:  1. date ___ kept going for ___ min
                     2. date ___ kept going for ___ min
                     3. date ___ kept going for ___ min
```

## Common mistakes

- **Calling yourself lazy.** Procrastination is usually avoiding a feeling. Find the feeling and shrink the task.
- **Waiting until you feel motivated.** Motivation often comes after starting. Start for five minutes.
- **Planning giant, vague tasks.** Write the first step so exactly that you could start without thinking.
- **Punishing yourself after a delay.** Forgive yourself and restart; harshness makes the next start harder.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. According to Sirois and Pychyl, what drives much procrastination?
    - A) A lack of intelligence
    - B) Too much sleep
    - C) Short-term mood repair: avoiding a task to feel better now
    - D) Knowing the subject too well
2. Which first step is best for a task you keep avoiding?
    - A) "Study maths properly this week"
    - B) "Master mental ability"
    - C) "Open the guide at page 34 and do five percentage questions"
    - D) "Be more disciplined"
3. What did the self-forgiveness study find?
    - A) Only harsh self-criticism helped
    - B) Self-forgiveness made students lazier
    - C) It had no effect on mood
    - D) Students who forgave themselves for procrastinating procrastinated less before their next exams
4. What is the five-minute start?
    - A) Taking a five-minute break before every task
    - B) Promising yourself only five minutes on the task, then deciding whether to continue
    - C) Studying for exactly five minutes a day
    - D) Reading for five hours

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Sirois and Pychyl's paper (abstract and introduction) and College Success 3.3 on procrastination
- **Action:** Keep a 5-day procrastination log and use the five-minute start on your most avoided task. It is done when your proof is saved: your 5-day procrastination log, notes from your three five-minute starts, and your self-forgiveness note.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **C.** Avoiding an unpleasant task improves mood now, while the cost falls on the future self.
2. **C.** A small, specific step makes the task less threatening and easier to start.
3. **D.** Wohl, Pychyl and Bennett (2010) followed 134 students through two sets of exams.
4. **B.** Starting is the hardest part; most people continue once they begin.

sections.title: LRN-M06-L02: Implementation intentions and tiny habits
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Write if-then plans for your key study habits and obstacles, shrink each habit to a tiny starter anchored to an existing routine, and track them in Loop Habit Tracker. **Time:** about 1 hour 15 minutes (20 minutes reading, 30 minutes resources, 25 minutes action plus 14 days of tracking).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Goals are not enough

"I will study more this month" is a **goal intention**. It names what you want, but not when, where or how. Most such goals fade within days.

An **implementation intention** is an if-then plan: **"If [situation], then I will [action]."** For example:

- "If it is 6 a.m. and I have poured my tea, then I will open AnkiDroid at the kitchen table."
- "If I sit down at the library after lunch, then I will start with a mixed set of 12 maths questions."

A meta-analysis of 94 independent tests found that forming implementation intentions had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals ([Gollwitzer and Sheeran, 2006](https://kops.uni-konstanz.de/entities/publication/2e749bfb-8533-437c-8203-7e788c910c5f)). That is one of the strongest findings in habit and motivation research, and it costs one sentence.

### If-then plans for obstacles

The same trick handles what usually derails you:

- "If a WhatsApp message arrives during a study block, then I will leave it until the break."
- "If there is a power cut at night, then I will switch to AnkiDroid and a paper recall of today's topic."
- "If I wake up late, then I will still do the 15-minute AnkiDroid review before anything else."

### Habits take time

A **habit** is an action that happens almost automatically in a familiar situation. Habits form by repeating the same action in the same context. Popular claims say a habit takes 21 days. In Dr Pippa Lally's research, forming a daily habit took **66 days on average**, with a very wide range, from 18 to 254 days ([University of Surrey, 2026](https://www.surrey.ac.uk/news/does-it-really-take-66-days-form-habit-we-asked-expert-dr-pippa-lally)). Expect weeks to months, and don't judge yourself at day 10.

### Tiny habits and anchors

Two ideas make new habits easier:

- **Make it tiny.** Start with a version so small it is hard to refuse: "open AnkiDroid and do 10 cards", "write three lines of recall", "solve one maths question". The tiny version builds the routine; on most days you will do more. This idea is popularised by B. J. Fogg's "Tiny Habits" method.
- **Anchor it to something you already do every day.** "After I pour my morning tea, I will open AnkiDroid." "After I return from the bus stop, I will do a five-minute recall." The existing routine becomes the "if".

### Track it with Loop

**Loop Habit Tracker** is a free, open-source Android app with reminders, charts and statistics ([Loop Habit Tracker](https://loophabits.org/)). Add only two or three habits at first: for example daily AnkiDroid, the morning study block, and the Sunday weekly review. Tick each day you do them. The chart makes progress visible and shows which days of the week are weak.

## Local example

**Sreeja** had tried to "study every day" many times. This time she wrote five if-then plans:

- If the children's school bus leaves, then I will sit at the dining table and open my Revision tab.
- If I have poured my evening tea, then I will do my AnkiDroid reviews before switching on the TV.
- If it is Sunday after lunch, then I will do my weekly review.
- If relatives visit during my morning slot, then I will do my reviews after they leave, before cooking.
- If I feel too tired at night, then I will do just 10 cards and sleep.

She installed Loop and added three habits with reminders. Her tiny versions were 10 cards, one Revision-tab review and three lines of weekly review. After 14 days Loop showed 13 out of 14 ticks for AnkiDroid, 11 for the morning slot and both Sunday reviews. The chart showed one weak day, Saturday, when her husband's family visits. She added an if-then plan for Saturdays.

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| If-then plans (implementation intentions) | **Strong** | Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006): a medium-to-large effect on goal attainment across 94 independent tests. |
| Habits take weeks to months to form | **Moderate** | Lally's research: an average of 66 days for a daily habit, ranging from 18 to 254. Based mainly on one well-known study. |
| Tiny habits anchored to existing routines | **Limited** | A popular method consistent with research on context cues and if-then plans; little direct testing. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [Gollwitzer and Sheeran (2006), implementation intentions meta-analysis (free PDF)](https://kops.uni-konstanz.de/entities/publication/2e749bfb-8533-437c-8203-7e788c910c5f) | Read the abstract and the summary of results | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [University of Surrey (21 January 2026): does it really take 66 days to form a habit? (Dr Pippa Lally)](https://www.surrey.ac.uk/news/does-it-really-take-66-days-form-habit-we-asked-expert-dr-pippa-lally) | Read the whole article on how long habits take | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Loop Habit Tracker (free, open source, GPLv3)](https://loophabits.org/) | Install Loop Habit Tracker and add your first habit | 10 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [College Success, chapter 3: Managing Your Time and Priorities (procrastination, time management, goals)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/03%3A_Managing_Your_Time_and_Priorities) | Read 3.6 Goal Setting and Motivation | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Write three if-then plans for study habits, each with a time or cue, a place and an action.
2. Write two if-then plans for the obstacles that most often derail you (use your procrastination log).
3. For each of the three habits, write its tiny version (two minutes or less) and the existing routine it follows.
4. Install Loop Habit Tracker, add the three habits with reminders at the right times, and tick them each day.
5. Track for 14 days (and keep going). On day 14, look at the chart, find your weakest day, and add an if-then plan for it.

**Proof to record:** Your five if-then plans with tiny versions and anchors, and a Loop screenshot after 14 days.

## Template: if-then planner

```
IF-THEN PLANS (implementation intentions)
Habits
1. If ________________________________ (time / cue), then I will ________________ at ____________ (place).
   Tiny version: ________________   Anchor (after I ...): ________________
2. If ________________________________, then I will ________________ at ____________.
   Tiny version: ________________   Anchor: ________________
3. If ________________________________, then I will ________________ at ____________.
   Tiny version: ________________   Anchor: ________________
Obstacles
4. If ________________________________ (obstacle), then I will ________________.
5. If ________________________________ (obstacle), then I will ________________.
```

## Template: Loop setup

```
[ ] Loop Habit Tracker installed
[ ] Habit 1: ______________  reminder at ____  days: every day
[ ] Habit 2: ______________  reminder at ____  days: ______
[ ] Habit 3: ______________  reminder at ____  days: Sunday
[ ] Ticked daily for 14 days
Day-14 check: weakest day ______  new if-then plan for it: _______________________
```

## Common mistakes

- **Vague plans ("study in the morning").** Name the cue, place and action: "after tea, at the kitchen table, AnkiDroid".
- **Starting ten habits at once.** Two or three habits first. Add more when these feel automatic.
- **Expecting a habit in 21 days.** The average in Lally's research was 66 days. Keep going past the first month.
- **Only planning for good days.** Write if-then plans for your usual obstacles too.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. Which is an implementation intention?
    - A) "I should use AnkiDroid more"
    - B) "I will study harder this month"
    - C) "I want to pass the PSC exam"
    - D) "If I have poured my morning tea, then I will open AnkiDroid at the kitchen table"
2. What did Gollwitzer and Sheeran's meta-analysis find?
    - A) They harm motivation
    - B) They work only for exercise
    - C) If-then plans had a medium-to-large effect on reaching goals across 94 tests
    - D) If-then plans had no effect
3. In Lally's research, how long did forming a daily habit take on average?
    - A) One week
    - B) About 66 days, ranging from 18 to 254
    - C) Exactly 21 days
    - D) One year for everyone
4. What is a good tiny version of "do AnkiDroid reviews every day"?
    - A) Review only on Sundays
    - B) Make 50 new cards a day
    - C) Do 500 cards every morning
    - D) Open AnkiDroid and do 10 cards after morning tea

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** Gollwitzer and Sheeran's abstract, the Surrey article on habits and College Success 3.6
- **Action:** Write five if-then plans, set up three tiny habits in Loop and track them for 14 days. It is done when your proof is saved: your five if-then plans with tiny versions and anchors, and a Loop screenshot after 14 days.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** It names the situation, the place and the action.
2. **C.** The reported effect size was d = 0.65.
3. **B.** Habits take weeks to months, and people vary widely.
4. **D.** A tiny version anchored to a routine is easy to start every day.

sections.title: LRN-M06-L03: Rewards, streaks and restarting after a bad week
sections.summary: **Outcome:** Use small rewards and streaks without letting them control you, connect daily study to your reasons, and restart quickly after a bad day or week. **Time:** about 1 hour (15 minutes reading, 20 minutes resources, 25 minutes action plus a week of rewards).
sections.content:
## Core lesson

### Motivation often follows action

Many people wait to feel motivated before they study. Often it works the other way round: you start, you make a little progress, and the progress makes you want to continue. The five-minute start (LRN-M06-L01) and tiny habits (LRN-M06-L02) use this. Motivation is helpful, but your system should work on days when you don't feel it.

### Rewards that help

The exam is months away; Reels are right here. A small, immediate reward after a study block gives your brain something now:

- A cup of tea or coffee, a short walk, a favourite song, a call with a friend, a sweet on Sundays
- **Pairing:** keep something you enjoy only for study-related moments, such as a favourite podcast only on the walk to the library

Two rules: the reward comes **after** the block, and it must not undo the work. An hour of Reels as a "reward" for a 25-minute block is a trap.

### Streaks: useful, with one rule

Loop and AnkiDroid show your streaks and calendars. A growing chain of ticks is motivating. The danger is **all-or-nothing thinking**: one missed day breaks the chain, you feel the streak is "ruined", and you stop for a week.

Use one rule: **never miss twice.** Missing one day is normal life. Missing two in a row starts a new habit: not studying. If you miss a day, the next day's tiny version is non-negotiable.

### Your reasons, and your process

Write down **why** you are doing this: a government job, security for your family, independence, pride, the subjects you enjoy. Read it on hard days. But don't rely only on the big outcome; it is far away and uncertain. Also take pride in the **process**: today's blocks done, this week's reviews done, this month's rising mock scores. Your Weekly tab and AnkiDroid statistics make the process visible.

### The restart protocol

Bad weeks will happen: illness, a wedding, exam stress, a family problem. What matters is how fast you restart.

1. **No guilt.** Forgive yourself (LRN-M06-L01); it makes restarting easier.
2. **Do the tiny version today,** not tomorrow and not "from Monday".
3. **Find what broke:** sleep, health, a family event, an unrealistic plan, stress.
4. **Adjust the plan:** fewer blocks, new cards to 0 in AnkiDroid until the backlog clears (LRN-M04-L04), one subject instead of three.
5. **Tell your study partner** or a family member, and agree on the next check-in.

If a bad week turns into weeks of low mood, exhaustion or dread, that is not a motivation problem; talk to someone you trust and see Module 19.

## Local example

**Ashiq** had a 23-day AnkiDroid streak when his cousin's wedding took over his family's life for five days. He didn't open the app once, and when he did, it showed 350 cards due. His first thought was, "The streak is gone, what's the point?"

His study partner Anu sent him the restart protocol from this lesson. He forgave himself (a wedding is a good reason), did the tiny version that same evening (10 cards), set new cards to 0, and did 20 minutes of reviews a day. He saw what had broken: no plan for family events. He added an if-then plan: "If there is a family function, then I will do 10 cards before leaving the house."

Within four days the backlog was gone. He started a new streak and wrote on the first page of his notebook: "Never miss twice." His reason card, taped inside the cover, says: "A permanent job, so Umma can stop working at the shop."

## How strong is the evidence?

| Technique or claim | Evidence | What the research says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Small immediate rewards after study | **Limited** | Consistent with basic research on reinforcement; little direct research with exam learners. |
| Forgiving yourself after a lapse | **Limited** | One study of 134 students (Wohl and others, 2010) found less later procrastination. |
| "Never miss twice" and restart protocols | **Limited** | Practical rules, consistent with Lally's finding that habit strength builds over many repetitions. |

## Free resources

| Resource | What to study | Time | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| [BPS Research Digest (4 May 2010): to cure procrastination, forgive yourself (Wohl, Pychyl and Bennett)](https://bps.org.uk/research-digest/cure-procrastination-forgive-yourself) | Reread the self-forgiveness study summary | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [College Success, chapter 3: Managing Your Time and Priorities (procrastination, time management, goals)](https://socialsci.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Counseling_and_Guidance/College_Success_%28OpenStax%29/03%3A_Managing_Your_Time_and_Priorities) | Reread 3.6 Goal Setting and Motivation, focusing on motivation | 15 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |
| [Loop Habit Tracker (free, open source, GPLv3)](https://loophabits.org/) | Look at your Loop charts and statistics for the last two weeks | 5 minutes | verified 2026-11-03 |

## Action task (on your PSC material)

1. Write your reason card: three lines on why you are preparing and learning. Keep it inside your notebook cover or as your phone's lock-screen note.
2. Write a reward menu of five small rewards that don't undo your work.
3. For one week, take one reward from the menu after each completed study block, and tick it.
4. Write your restart protocol (use the template) and keep it in your notebook.
5. Look at your Loop and AnkiDroid records. Find the day of the week you are most likely to miss, and write an if-then plan for it.

**Proof to record:** Your reason card, your reward menu with a week of ticks, your restart protocol and your weak-day if-then plan.

## Template: reward menu

```
REWARD MENU (small, immediate, after the block, never undoing the work)
1. ____________________ (e.g. tea on the verandah)
2. ____________________ (e.g. a 10-minute walk)
3. ____________________ (e.g. one favourite song)
4. ____________________ (e.g. a call with a friend)
5. ____________________ (e.g. Sunday sweet after the weekly review)
Pairing: I only ____________________ when I ____________________.
Week: Mon [ ] Tue [ ] Wed [ ] Thu [ ] Fri [ ] Sat [ ] Sun [ ]
```

## Template: restart protocol

```
RESTART PROTOCOL (after a bad day or week)
1. Forgive: "I missed ____ because ____. That is human."
2. Tiny version TODAY: ______________________ (not "from Monday")
3. What broke? sleep / health / family event / unrealistic plan / stress / other: ____
4. Adjust: blocks ___ -> ___ ; AnkiDroid new cards -> 0 until due count < ___ ; subjects: ____
5. Tell: ______________ (study partner or family). Next check-in: ______
Rule: never miss twice.
```

## Common mistakes

- **Rewards that undo the work.** An hour of scrolling after 25 minutes of study is a trap. Keep rewards small and short.
- **Treating a broken streak as failure.** Never miss twice. One missed day is normal.
- **Restarting "from Monday".** Do the tiny version today.
- **Relying only on the big goal for motivation.** Track and celebrate the process: blocks, reviews, rising scores.

## Quiz

Answer from memory first: that is retrieval practice. The answers are at the bottom of this page.

1. What does the "never miss twice" rule mean?
    - A) You must never miss a single day
    - B) Miss two days, then restart on Monday
    - C) Study twice as much after missing a day
    - D) Missing one day is normal; the next day's tiny version is non-negotiable
2. Which is a good reward after a 25-minute study block?
    - A) An hour of Reels
    - B) Buying an expensive gadget
    - C) Skipping the next block
    - D) A cup of tea and a short walk
3. After a bad week, what is the first step of the restart protocol?
    - A) Forgive yourself
    - B) Plan a 12-hour study day
    - C) Wait for Monday
    - D) Delete your decks and start fresh
4. Why track the process (blocks, reviews, scores) and not only the exam goal?
    - A) Process tracking replaces studying
    - B) The exam goal doesn't matter
    - C) Goals reduce motivation
    - D) The goal is far away and uncertain; visible daily progress keeps you going

## Progress checklist

Tick these under **Your tasks** at the top of this page:

- **Study:** The self-forgiveness summary, College Success 3.6 and your own Loop charts
- **Action:** Write your reason card, reward menu and restart protocol, and use rewards for a week. It is done when your proof is saved: your reason card, your reward menu with a week of ticks, your restart protocol and your weak-day if-then plan.
- **Quiz:** at least 3 right, or re-read the core lesson and try again tomorrow.

## Answers

1. **D.** It keeps one lapse from becoming a new habit of not studying.
2. **D.** Small and immediate, and it doesn't undo the work.
3. **A.** Guilt makes restarting harder; forgiveness clears the way.
4. **D.** Seeing progress now supports motivation between now and the exam.

sections.summary: Retake the four tests with fresh versions, compare with week 0, and check that every part of your learning system exists and runs.
sections.content:
Two things finish the course: retake the four tests with fresh versions, and check that every part of your learning system exists and runs.

## 1. Retake the tests (form B)

Use exactly the same steps, timing and conditions as in week 0, but with the form B materials below. This time, **use any technique you learned**: that is the point. Fill in the **End** column of the Baseline tab, then the **Change** column.

When you compare, be fair to yourself:

- **Some improvement comes from practice:** you have done these tests before. The big gains (often in list recall) come from technique.
- **Digit span may not move.** That's normal (see **Start here**). If it did, write down the strategy you used.
- **Write three lines:** your biggest gain, the method behind it, and one score you want to improve next.

## Test 1: the 20-item list (about 20 minutes, plus 3 minutes tomorrow)

1. Have a pen, paper and a timer ready. Set the timer for **2 minutes**.
2. Start the timer and study the list below in any way you like. Stop when the timer rings.
3. Cover the list. For the next **10 minutes**, do something that keeps your mind busy, such as arithmetic questions from your PSC book. Don't rehearse the list.
4. Write down every word you remember, in any order, in **3 minutes**. Count the correct words (spelling doesn't matter). That is your **10-minute score**.
5. **Don't look at the list again.** Exactly 24 hours later, write the words again in 3 minutes, without looking. That is your **24-hour score**.

```
LIST B (study for 2 minutes)
 1. hammer
 2. lion
 3. lantern
 4. garlic
 5. scooter
 6. envelope
 7. flute
 8. jackfruit
 9. spade
10. blanket
11. lock
12. basket
13. peacock
14. needle
15. train
16. comb
17. chain
18. pumpkin
19. balloon
20. cup
```

## Test 2: reading speed and comprehension (about 15 minutes)

1. Read the passage below **once**, at your normal pace for understanding: not skimming, not studying. Time yourself with the stopwatch from the first word to the last.
2. Without looking back, answer the 8 questions below it.
3. Work out your scores:
    - **Reading speed (wpm)** = 542 words ÷ your minutes. Example: 3 minutes 20 seconds is 3.33 minutes, so 542 ÷ 3.33 = 163 wpm.
    - **Comprehension %** = correct answers ÷ 8 × 100
    - **Effective reading rate** = wpm × comprehension % ÷ 100

### Passage B: The ferry at Kannankadavu (542 words)

For thirty-one years, the only way to cross the river at Kannankadavu without a long walk to the bridge downstream was Ummer's ferry. The ferry was a wide country boat that could carry twelve people, or eight people and two bicycles. Ummer pushed it across with a long bamboo pole, and on a calm day the crossing took about six minutes.

He had taken over the ferry from his uncle in 1987. The panchayat owned the crossing and leased it every three years to whoever offered the most money. Ummer kept the lease by doing one thing better than anyone else: he was never late. Schoolchildren, fish sellers and office workers set their watches by the first crossing at six in the morning. He charged fifty paise a person when he started and three rupees by the end, and children in school uniform always crossed free. On Fridays, when the market on the far bank was busiest, he made an extra crossing every half hour until noon, and his wife sold boiled peanuts in paper cones to the people waiting at the landing.

The monsoon was the hardest season. When the water rose above a mark he had painted on a coconut tree, Ummer stopped the ferry, however many people were waiting. Some passengers shouted at him. Once, in 1994, a man offered him a hundred rupees to cross in a flood. Ummer refused. That evening a branch the size of a lorry came down the river past the exact spot where the boat would have been. After that, nobody argued with the coconut tree.

In 2009 the government announced that a bridge would be built at Kannankadavu. Everyone expected Ummer to be angry, since the bridge would end his work. Instead he went to the engineers' office and asked to see the plans. The engineers were surprised; most visitors came only to complain about the noise. He noticed that the bridge would be built about two hundred metres upstream, close to a temple path, so people from his side would still have to walk past his landing to reach it. He used his savings to start a tea stall at the landing, and he began serving tea to the construction workers.

The bridge took six years instead of the two that had been promised. During that time the tea stall slowly became more important than the ferry. Ummer added newspapers, a bench and, later, a small shelf of snacks. When the bridge finally opened in 2015, he sold the boat to a tourism group that wanted it for evening rides.

Not all of his ideas worked. He tried to sell fish from the stall, but the smell kept tea customers away, and he stopped after a month. A plan to rent out bicycles to people crossing the new bridge failed because almost everyone already owned one.

Today his daughter Shabna runs the stall, which now has four tables and a name for the best banana fritters on that stretch of road. Ummer still sits on the bench every morning at six. When people ask whether he misses the ferry, he points at the river and says, "The river did not stop. I only changed which side of it I stood on."

### Questions on passage B

1. How long did the crossing take on a calm day?
    - A) About two minutes
    - B) About thirty minutes
    - C) About ten minutes
    - D) About six minutes
2. How did Ummer keep the ferry lease?
    - A) He was never late
    - B) He carried bicycles free
    - C) He was related to a panchayat member
    - D) He always offered the most money
3. What did Ummer do when the water rose above the mark on the coconut tree?
    - A) He doubled the fare
    - B) He stopped the ferry
    - C) He used a bigger boat
    - D) He carried only children
4. Why did nobody argue with the coconut tree after 1994?
    - A) The tree was carried away by the flood
    - B) A huge branch came down the river where the boat would have been
    - C) Ummer bought a stronger boat
    - D) The panchayat made a new rule
5. Why did Ummer start a tea stall at the landing?
    - A) The tourism group paid him to start it
    - B) His uncle had once run a tea stall there
    - C) The engineers asked him to feed their workers
    - D) He saw that people would still walk past his landing to reach the new bridge
6. How long did the bridge take to build?
    - A) Three years
    - B) Six years
    - C) Two years
    - D) Nine years
7. Why did the bicycle rental plan fail?
    - A) The bicycles were stolen
    - B) Bicycles were not allowed on the bridge
    - C) It cost too much to start
    - D) Almost everyone already owned a bicycle
8. Which of these is NOT stated in the passage?
    - A) The boat was sold to a tourism group
    - B) Ummer received compensation from the government for losing the ferry
    - C) Ummer's daughter now runs the stall
    - D) Children in school uniform crossed free

## Test 3: focus duration (45 minutes, on two different days)

1. Choose a normal PSC study task: reading a new chapter and making notes works well.
2. Set up the way you **usually** study. Don't change anything for the test.
3. Start the stopwatch. Study for 45 minutes. Keep a paper beside you: every time you notice your attention left the task (you checked the phone, got up, started daydreaming), make a tally mark. Write down the time of the **first** one.
4. Record: **minutes to first distraction**, **number of tally marks**, and a focus rating from 1 to 10.
5. Repeat on another day this week, and use the average of the two.

## Test 4: digit span (10 minutes, with a helper if possible)

**With a helper (best):** the helper reads each line aloud at about one digit per second, in a flat voice. You repeat the digits (forward: same order; backward: reverse order). Start at the shortest lines. Stop a section when you fail **both** lines of the same length.

**Alone:** cover the list with a paper and slide it down to show one line for as many seconds as there are digits, cover it again, and write the digits down. Use the same method again in week 28, so the scores compare fairly.

**Your span** in each section is the longest length where you got at least one of the two lines exactly right.

## Part 5: your learning habits (5 minutes)

Rate each statement: **1** never, **2** rarely, **3** sometimes, **4** usually, **5** almost always. Add them up (out of 75).

sections.title: What next: keep your learning system running
sections.summary: Daily, weekly and 12-weekly routines after the course, and how to use the same system for AI skills, business, money and new languages.
sections.content:
Finishing the course is the start of running your own learning system. Here is how to keep it going, for PSC and after it.

## Every day (20–60 minutes)

- AnkiDroid reviews first, then new cards only if the reviews are done.
- One retrieval session on your main PSC topic: blank-page recall or practice questions, before any rereading.
- Phone out of reach during study blocks.

## Every week (20 minutes)

- The weekly learning review. One change at a time.
- Update the Revision tab and clear the Errors tab's retests.

## Every 12 weeks (one evening)

- Review your 12-week PSC plan (LRN-M12-L05): what is solid, what is weak, and the next cycle's priorities.
- Take one full mock test under exam conditions, and analyse it with the error log.
- Repeat one of the baseline tests (form A works again by now), to keep measuring.

## After PSC: the same system, new subjects

| What you want to learn | Where to start | Methods to use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AI skills | The Free AI Generalist Course in this app | A learning project plan (LRN-M13-L02), Feynman explanations of each new idea, AnkiDroid for terms |
| Starting a business | Practical Entrepreneurship in this app | Deliberate practice with real customers, feedback loops, a weekly review |
| Marketing and freelancing | Practical Social Media Marketing in this app | Interleaved practice on real posts, an error log of what failed |
| Money management | Practical Personal Finance in this app | Concrete examples with your own numbers, spaced review of key rules |
| A new language (Hindi, Arabic, German...) | [Language Transfer](https://www.languagetransfer.org/) (free audio courses) and the LRN-M15-L04 plan | Daily input, shadowing, a vocabulary deck in AnkiDroid |
| Better English | [British Council LearnEnglish](https://learnenglish.britishcouncil.org/) | Reading and listening every day, a phrase deck, speaking practice with a partner |
| How learning works, in more depth | [Learning How to Learn](https://www.coursera.org/learn/learning-how-to-learn) on Coursera (free to enrol) | Take notes as questions; make cards for key ideas |

## Keep learning about learning, free

- [The Learning Scientists](https://www.learningscientists.org/downloadable-materials): posters, slides and a blog on the six strategies
- [RetrievalPractice.org](https://www.retrievalpractice.org/): guides and research summaries
- [How To Remember Anything Forever-ish](https://ncase.me/remember/): the best 20-minute refresher on spaced repetition
- [OpenStax Psychology 2e](https://openstax.org/books/psychology-2e/pages/preface), chapters 7 and 8 on thinking and memory

## A warning about "learning hacks"

You will meet videos and apps that promise photographic memory, 1,000 words a minute, or "brain training" that raises intelligence. Check them against what you learned in Module 2 and the evidence tables in this course. The methods that work are less exciting: recall, spacing, mixing, explaining, sleep, and doing it every week.

Every link on this page was checked on 2026-11-03; see the **Sources and verification log** for each one's status.

sections.title: Glossary with Malayalam meanings
sections.summary: 74 key learning terms in English and Malayalam, with simple meanings.
sections.content:
Key words from the course, roughly in the order you meet them. Many English terms, such as AnkiDroid, mock test and PYQ, are used as they are in Malayalam conversation; the Malayalam is given so you can explain them to family and study partners.

| English | മലയാളം (Malayalam) | Simple meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Learning** | പഠനം | A lasting change in what you know or can do |
| **Attention** | ശ്രദ്ധ | Choosing what your mind works on right now |
| **Working memory** | പ്രവർത്തന ഓർമ്മ (താൽക്കാലിക ഓർമ്മ) | The small mental "desk" that holds a few items for seconds while you use them |
| **Long-term memory** | ദീർഘകാല ഓർമ്മ | Your large, lasting store of knowledge and skills |
| **Cognitive load** | ബൗദ്ധിക ഭാരം | How much a task demands from working memory |
| **Schema** | അറിവിന്റെ ചട്ടക്കൂട് | An organised pattern of knowledge in long-term memory |
| **Encoding** | ഓർമ്മയിൽ പതിപ്പിക്കൽ | Turning what you experience into a memory |
| **Consolidation** | ഓർമ്മ ഉറപ്പിക്കൽ | The brain stabilising new memories over hours and during sleep |
| **Retrieval** | ഓർത്തെടുക്കൽ | Bringing a memory back to mind |
| **Forgetting curve** | മറവിയുടെ വക്രരേഖ | Memory loss that is fast at first and slower later |
| **Neuroplasticity** | ന്യൂറോപ്ലാസ്റ്റിസിറ്റി (തലച്ചോറിന് മാറാനുള്ള കഴിവ്) | The brain changing its connections with learning and experience |
| **Chunk** | കൂട്ടം (ചങ്ക്) | Several items grouped and remembered as one unit |
| **Neuromyth** | തലച്ചോറിനെക്കുറിച്ചുള്ള മിഥ്യാധാരണ | A popular but false belief about the brain |
| **Learning styles** | പഠന ശൈലികൾ | The unsupported idea that teaching should match "visual" or "auditory" learners |
| **Illusion of knowing** | അറിവിന്റെ മിഥ്യാബോധം | Feeling that you know something because it looks familiar |
| **Retrieval practice** | ഓർത്തെടുക്കൽ പരിശീലനം | Learning by recalling without looking |
| **Spaced practice** | ഇടവിട്ടുള്ള പഠനം | Spreading study over days and weeks instead of cramming |
| **Interleaving** | ഇടകലർത്തിയുള്ള പരിശീലനം | Mixing different types of problems in one practice session |
| **Elaboration** | വിശദീകരിച്ചുള്ള പഠനം | Asking how and why, and linking new ideas to what you know |
| **Concrete example** | മൂർത്തമായ ഉദാഹരണം | A specific case that shows an abstract idea |
| **Dual coding** | ഇരട്ട കോഡിങ് (വാക്കും ചിത്രവും) | Combining words with pictures, maps, timelines or diagrams |
| **Spaced repetition** | ഇടവേള ആവർത്തനം | Reviewing at growing intervals, timed by software |
| **Flashcard** | ഓർമ്മക്കാർഡ് (ഫ്ലാഷ്കാർഡ്) | A card with a question on one side and the answer on the other |
| **Cloze deletion** | വിട്ടഭാഗം പൂരിപ്പിക്കൽ | A card that hides one word or phrase in a sentence |
| **Image occlusion** | ചിത്രഭാഗം മറയ്ക്കൽ | A card that hides part of a map or diagram |
| **Deck** | കാർഡ് ശേഖരം (ഡെക്ക്) | A collection of flashcards |
| **Retention** | ഓർമ്മ നിലനിർത്തൽ നിരക്ക് | The share of reviews you answer correctly |
| **Leech** | ആവർത്തിച്ച് തെറ്റുന്ന കാർഡ് (ലീച്ച്) | A card you keep failing; rewrite or split it |
| **Focus** | ഏകാഗ്രത | Keeping attention on one task |
| **Distraction** | ശ്രദ്ധ തെറ്റൽ | Anything that pulls your attention away |
| **Multitasking** | ഒരേസമയം പല ജോലികൾ | Switching quickly between tasks; it costs accuracy and time |
| **Deep work** | ആഴത്തിലുള്ള ജോലി | Long, undistracted work on a demanding task |
| **Time-blocking** | സമയം മുൻകൂട്ടി വിഭജിക്കൽ | Giving each task a fixed slot in your day |
| **Procrastination** | നീട്ടിവയ്ക്കൽ | Delaying a task you intend to do, even though delay will cost you |
| **Implementation intention** | എങ്കിൽ-അപ്പോൾ പദ്ധതി | A plan in the form "If X happens, then I will do Y" |
| **Habit** | ശീലം | An action done almost automatically in a familiar situation |
| **Motivation** | പ്രചോദനം | The reasons and energy that move you to act |
| **Metacognition** | മെറ്റാകോഗ്നിഷൻ (സ്വന്തം പഠനത്തെക്കുറിച്ചുള്ള ബോധം) | Knowing, checking and managing your own learning |
| **Calibration** | ആത്മവിലയിരുത്തലിന്റെ കൃത്യത | How well your confidence matches your real accuracy |
| **Self-explanation** | സ്വയം വിശദീകരണം | Explaining each step or idea to yourself as you study |
| **Feynman technique** | ഫെയ്ൻമാൻ രീതി | Explaining a topic simply, aloud, to find and fix the gaps |
| **Concept map** | ആശയ ഭൂപടം | Ideas in boxes joined by labelled arrows |
| **First principles** | അടിസ്ഥാന തത്ത്വങ്ങൾ | The basic truths from which you can rebuild an idea |
| **Cornell notes** | കോർണൽ കുറിപ്പ് രീതി | A page with notes, a question column and a summary |
| **Mind map** | മനോഭൂപടം (മൈൻഡ് മാപ്പ്) | A central topic with branches of related ideas |
| **Skimming** | ഓടിച്ചു വായിക്കൽ | Reading fast for the main idea |
| **Scanning** | തിരഞ്ഞു വായിക്കൽ | Searching a text quickly for one specific fact |
| **Comprehension** | ഗ്രഹണശേഷി | Understanding what you read |
| **Mnemonic** | ഓർമ്മസൂത്രം | A trick that makes something easier to remember |
| **Memory palace (method of loci)** | ഓർമ്മക്കൊട്ടാരം (സ്ഥാനരീതി) | Placing vivid images along a familiar route to remember a list |
| **Peg system** | കൊളുത്ത് രീതി (പെഗ് സിസ്റ്റം) | Hanging items on a memorised list of number-images |
| **Major system** | മേജർ സിസ്റ്റം (അക്കം-വ്യഞ്ജനം രീതി) | Turning digits into consonant sounds, then into words |
| **Syllabus** | പാഠ്യപദ്ധതി (സിലബസ്) | The official list of topics for an exam |
| **Previous-year questions (PYQ)** | മുൻവർഷ ചോദ്യങ്ങൾ | Questions from past papers of the same or similar exams |
| **Mock test** | മാതൃകാ പരീക്ഷ | A practice exam under real exam conditions |
| **Error log** | തെറ്റുകളുടെ രേഖ | A record of your mistakes, their causes and fixes |
| **Negative marking** | നെഗറ്റീവ് മാർക്ക് | Marks deducted for wrong answers |
| **Revision** | പുനരവലോകനം (റിവിഷൻ) | Going back over what you learned, best done by recall |
| **Deliberate practice** | ബോധപൂർവമായ പരിശീലനം | Focused practice on weak points, with feedback |
| **Feedback** | പ്രതികരണം (ഫീഡ്ബാക്ക്) | Information on how you did and what to fix |
| **Critical thinking** | വിമർശനാത്മക ചിന്ത | Judging claims by their evidence and reasoning |
| **Argument** | വാദം | Reasons (premises) offered in support of a conclusion |
| **Fallacy** | തെറ്റായ വാദരീതി | A flawed argument that can still sound convincing |
| **Cognitive bias** | ചിന്താ പക്ഷപാതം | A systematic error in thinking |
| **Mental model** | മാനസിക മാതൃക | A simple idea that helps explain how something works |
| **Comprehensible input** | മനസ്സിലാകുന്ന ഭാഷാ ഇൻപുട്ട് | Listening or reading that you can mostly understand |
| **Shadowing** | ഷാഡോയിങ് (കേട്ട് ഒപ്പം പറയൽ) | Repeating audio aloud right after the speaker |
| **Vocabulary** | പദസമ്പത്ത് | The words you know and can use |
| **Hallucination (AI)** | എഐയുടെ സാങ്കൽപ്പിക ഉത്തരം | An AI tool stating something false as if it were true |
| **Socratic questioning** | സോക്രട്ടീസിയൻ ചോദ്യരീതി | Teaching by asking questions that make you think |
| **Knowledge base** | വിജ്ഞാന ശേഖരം | Your linked collection of notes |
| **Stress** | മാനസിക സമ്മർദ്ദം | The body's response to demands or threats |

Every link in this course is listed here with the date it was checked. Links were opened and read on 2026-11-03; nothing here was copied from memory. If a link stops working, search for its title on the same website.

- **verified 2026-11-03:** the page was opened on that date and its content matched what the course says.
- **verified 2026-11-03; check current rules:** as above, but it describes something that changes: an app feature, an exam rule or a syllabus. Open the source before you rely on it.
- **unverified:** the site blocks automated checks, so the page could not be opened for this course. The address is the official one; type it yourself and check that it is the real site.

Official and open-licensed sources are preferred: OpenStax books (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0), the public-domain comic by Nicky Case, open-access papers, and open-source apps (AnkiDroid, Joplin, Logseq, Loop). This course only links to them. Where a paper is behind a paywall, the course links to a free summary by the university or society that published it, and says so in the title.
